title: Part 1, Chapter 12
paragraphs: What a goatherd told the company with Don Quixote
Just then another young man arrived, one of those who carried provisions up from the village, and he said, "Do you know what's happening in the village, friends?"
"How would we know?" one of them replied.

"Well, listen to this," the young man went on. "This morning that famous student-shepherd named Chrysostom died, and the rumor is that he died of love for that devil of a village girl, the daughter of Guillermo the Rich — the one who roams the open country around here dressed as a shepherdess."
"You mean Marcela?" said one of them.

"That's the one," the goatherd answered. "And here's the strangest part: he stated in his will that he wants to be buried out in the fields, like a Moor, at the foot of the rock by the Cork-tree spring, because — so the story goes, and they say he said it himself — that was the spot where he first laid eyes on her. He left other instructions too, which the village clergy say should not and must not be carried out, because they smack of paganism. But his great friend Ambrosio, the student who dressed as a shepherd alongside him, insists that everything must be done exactly as Chrysostom directed, with nothing left out, and the whole village is in an uproar over it. Still, word is that in the end Ambrosio and his shepherd friends will get their way, and tomorrow they're coming to bury him with great ceremony in the place I mentioned. I'm sure it will be something worth seeing; at any rate, I won't miss it, even if I knew I couldn't get back to the village tomorrow."
"We'll all do the same," the goatherds answered, "and we'll draw lots to see who has to stay behind and watch everyone's goats."

"Good thinking, Pedro," said one, "though there's no need to go to that trouble — I'll stay behind for all of you. And don't put it down to virtue or a lack of curiosity on my part; it's just that the splinter that went into my foot the other day won't let me walk."
"We thank you all the same," Pedro answered.

Don Quixote asked Pedro to tell him who the dead man was and who the shepherdess was. Pedro replied that all he knew was that the dead man had been a wealthy gentleman from a village in those mountains who had studied at Salamanca for many years and then come home with a reputation for being very learned and widely read. "Above all, people said, he was an expert in the science of the stars and everything that goes on up there in the sky with the sun and the moon — he used to tell us the cris of the sun and moon down to the exact moment."

"It's called an eclipse, my friend, not a cris — the darkening of those two great lights," said Don Quixote. But Pedro, not bothering with such trifles, carried on with his story: "He also predicted when a year was going to bring abundance or estility."
"Sterility, you mean," said Don Quixote.

"Sterility or estility," Pedro answered, "it comes to the same thing in the end. And I can tell you that his father and the friends who trusted him got very rich by following his advice, because he would tell them: 'Sow barley this year, not wheat; this year you can plant beans but not barley; next year there'll be a bumper olive crop, and for the three years after that you won't get a drop of oil.'"
"That science is called astrology," said Don Quixote.

"I don't know what it's called," Pedro replied, "but I do know he knew all that and more besides. Anyway, to cut it short: not many months after he came back from Salamanca, he showed up one day dressed as a shepherd, with a crook and a sheepskin, having thrown off the long gown he'd worn as a scholar; and at the same time his great friend Ambrosio, who had been his companion in his studies, put on shepherd's clothes along with him. I forgot to mention that Chrysostom, the one who's dead, was a great hand at writing verses — so much so that he wrote the carols for Christmas Eve and the plays for Corpus Christi that the young men of our village performed, and everyone said they were excellent. When the villagers saw the two scholars suddenly appear in shepherd's dress, they were astonished and couldn't guess what had driven them to such a bizarre change. Around this time our Chrysostom's father died, and he inherited a great deal of property, in goods as well as land, no small number of cattle and sheep, and a large sum of money. The young man was left absolute master of all of it, and honestly, he deserved every bit, because he was a very good companion, kind-hearted, a friend to decent people, and with a face like a blessing. Before long it came out that he had changed his clothes for no other reason than to wander these wild places chasing after that shepherdess Marcela our lad mentioned a moment ago, because the late Chrysostom had fallen in love with her. And now I must tell you — because you ought to know — who this girl is. Perhaps, or rather without any perhaps, you'll never have heard anything like it in all the days of your life, even if you live more years than sarna."
"Say Sarra," said Don Quixote, unable to bear the goatherd's mangling of words.
"The sarna lives long enough," Pedro answered, "and if you're going to pick at my words at every step, señor, we won't be finished within a year."

"Forgive me, friend," said Don Quixote. "I only mentioned it because there's such a difference between sarna and Sarra. But you've answered very well, since the sarna does outlive Sarra — so go on with your story, and I won't object to anything else."

"Well then, my dear sir," said the goatherd, "in our village there was a farmer even richer than Chrysostom's father, named Guillermo, and God gave him, on top of his great wealth, a daughter whose mother died giving birth to her — and she was the most respected woman in this whole district. I can picture her even now, with that face that seemed to carry the sun on one side and the moon on the other; and on top of that she was hardworking and kind to the poor, which is why I trust her soul is at this very moment in bliss with God in the next world. Her husband Guillermo died of grief at losing such a good wife, leaving his daughter Marcela, a child and an heiress, in the care of one of her uncles, a priest who held a benefice in our village. The girl grew up so beautiful that she reminded us of her mother, whose beauty was remarkable — and yet people thought the daughter's would surpass it. And so it was that when she reached fourteen or fifteen, nobody could look at her without blessing God for making her so beautiful, and most of them fell hopelessly in love with her. Her uncle kept her closely sheltered and out of sight, but even so, the fame of her great beauty spread until, both for that and for her great fortune, her uncle was asked, pressed, and pestered to give her in marriage — not only by men from our town but by men from many leagues around, including some of the highest standing among them. But being a good Christian, although he wanted to marry her off promptly once he saw she was of age, he refused to do it without her consent — and not because he had any eye on the income and profit her property brought him while he kept putting off her marriage. And believe me, this was said in praise of the good priest in more than one circle in town. Because I'd have you know, Sir Errant, that in these little villages everything gets talked about and everything gets criticized, and you can be as sure as I am that a priest has to be exceptionally good before he can force his parishioners to speak well of him — especially in villages."
"That's the truth," said Don Quixote, "but go on, for the story is very good, and you, good Pedro, tell it with real style."

"May the Lord's grace never fail me," said Pedro, "that's the style that matters. To continue: you should know that although the uncle laid out for his niece the qualities of each one of her many suitors in particular, urging her to marry and choose whichever suited her own taste, she never gave any answer except that she had no wish to marry yet, and that being so young, she didn't feel ready to carry the burden of married life. Faced with these apparently reasonable excuses, her uncle stopped pressing her and decided to wait until she was a bit older and could choose a partner to her own liking. Because, he said — and he was quite right — parents shouldn't force their children into a settled life against their will. But then, when no one expected it, what do you know — one day the demure Marcela appears, transformed into a shepherdess; and despite her uncle and everyone in town who tried to talk her out of it, she took to going out into the fields with the other shepherd girls of the village and tending her own flock. And from the moment she appeared in public and her beauty could be seen in the open, I honestly couldn't tell you how many rich young men, gentlemen and farmers alike, have put on Chrysostom's kind of costume and gone roaming these fields courting her. One of them, as I've already said, was our dead friend, who people say didn't just love her but worshipped her. But don't imagine, just because Marcela chose a life of such freedom and independence, with little privacy or rather none at all, that she has given the slightest occasion — or even the appearance of one — to cast doubt on her purity and modesty. On the contrary, she guards her honor with such vigilance, and so much of it, that of all the men who court and pursue her, not one has boasted, or could truthfully boast, that she ever gave him the smallest hope of getting what he wanted. For although she doesn't avoid or shun the company and conversation of the shepherds, and treats them with courtesy and kindness, the moment any one of them comes to declare his intentions — even intentions as proper and holy as marriage — she hurls him away from her like a catapult. And with this temperament of hers she does more damage in this country than if the plague had broken out in it, because her friendliness and her beauty draw the hearts of those around her into loving and courting her, while her scorn and her plain speaking drive them to the edge of despair; so they don't know what to say except to call her out loud cruel and hard-hearted, and other names of that sort that describe her character well enough. And if you stayed here any length of time, señor, you would hear these hills and valleys echoing with the laments of the rejected men who chase after her. Not far from here there's a spot with a couple of dozen tall beech trees, and there isn't one of them that doesn't have the name of Marcela carved and written into its smooth bark — and above some of them a crown carved into the same tree, as if her admirer wanted to say more plainly still that Marcela wears and deserves the crown of all human beauty. Here one shepherd sighs, there another grieves; over there you hear love songs, over here despairing laments. One of them will spend all the hours of the night sitting at the foot of some oak or rock, and the sun finds him there in the morning, his weeping eyes never having closed, dazed and out of his senses; another, giving his sighs no rest or relief, lies stretched on the burning sand in the full heat of the sweltering summer noon, sending up his appeal to the merciful heavens — and over this one and that one, over these and all of them, the beautiful Marcela triumphs, free and unconcerned. All of us who know her are waiting to see where her pride will end, and who the lucky man will be who manages to tame so formidable a nature and take possession of a beauty so supreme. Since everything I've told you is well-established fact, I'm convinced that what they say about the cause of Chrysostom's death, the way our lad told it, is the truth as well. So I advise you, señor, don't fail to be at his burial tomorrow. It will be well worth watching, because Chrysostom had many friends, and the place where he asked to be buried isn't half a league from here."
"I'll make a point of it," said Don Quixote, "and I thank you for the pleasure you've given me by telling such a fascinating story."

"Oh," said the goatherd, "I don't know even half of what has happened to Marcela's lovers, but perhaps tomorrow we'll run into some shepherd on the road who can tell us. For now you'd do well to go and sleep under a roof, because the night air could harm your wound — though with the remedy I've put on it, there's no fear of any complication."

Sancho Panza, who was wishing the goatherd's endless talking to the devil, urged his master for his part to come and sleep in Pedro's hut. He did so, and spent the whole rest of the night thinking about his lady Dulcinea, in imitation of Marcela's lovers. Sancho Panza settled himself down between Rocinante and his donkey and slept — not like a rejected lover, but like a man who had been thoroughly kicked.

title: Part 1, Chapter 13
paragraphs: In which the story of the shepherdess Marcela is concluded, along with other events

But day had barely begun to show itself through the balconies of the east when five of the six goatherds came to wake Don Quixote and tell him that if he was still inclined to go and see Chrysostom's famous burial, they would keep him company. Don Quixote wanted nothing more. He got up and ordered Sancho to saddle up and load the packsaddle at once, which he did at top speed, and just as quickly they all set out together. They had not gone a quarter of a league when, at a point where two paths met, they saw about six shepherds coming toward them, dressed in black sheepskins, their heads crowned with garlands of cypress and bitter oleander. Each carried a stout holly staff in his hand, and along with them came two gentlemen on horseback in handsome traveling clothes, accompanied by three servants on foot. The two groups exchanged courteous greetings when they met, and after asking one another where each party was headed, they learned that everyone was bound for the burial site, so they all rode on together.

One of the riders, addressing his companion, said to him, “It seems to me, Señor Vivaldo, that we can count as time well spent the delay we'll take on by seeing this remarkable funeral — and remarkable it must be, judging by the strange things these shepherds have told us about both the dead shepherd and the homicidal shepherdess.”
“That's what I think too,” Vivaldo replied, “and I would hold up my journey not just one day but four for the sake of seeing it.”

Don Quixote asked them what they had heard about Marcela and Chrysostom. The traveler answered that they had run into these shepherds that same morning and, seeing them dressed in such mournful style, had asked the reason why they were going around looking that way. One of them had explained, describing the strange behavior and beauty of a shepherdess called Marcela, the loves of the many men who courted her, and the death of this Chrysostom, to whose burial they were now heading. In short, he repeated everything Pedro had told Don Quixote.

That conversation ended, and another began when the man called Vivaldo asked Don Quixote what reason he had for going around armed like that in such a peaceful country. Don Quixote answered, “The pursuit of my calling does not allow or permit me to travel any other way. An easy life, pleasure, and rest were invented for soft courtiers; but toil, restlessness, and arms were invented and made only for those whom the world calls knights-errant — of whom I, though unworthy, am the least of all.”

The moment they heard this, they all sized him up as a madman; and to settle the point more firmly and discover what kind of madness this was, Vivaldo went on to ask him what exactly “knights-errant” meant.

“Haven't you gentlemen,” Don Quixote replied, “read the annals and histories of England, which record the famous deeds of King Arthur — the one we in our everyday Castilian always call King Artus? About him there is an ancient tradition, accepted throughout that kingdom of Great Britain, that this king did not die but was changed by magic art into a raven, and that in due time he will return to reign and reclaim his kingdom and scepter — which is why it cannot be proved that, from that day to this, any Englishman has ever killed a raven. Well then, it was in the time of this good king that the famous chivalric order of the Knights of the Round Table was founded, and the love affair of Don Lancelot of the Lake with Queen Guinevere took place exactly as the histories relate it, the go-between and confidante being the highly honorable lady Quintañona — which gave us that ballad so well known and widely sung in our Spain —

Oh, never was there any knight
 so waited on by lady's hand,
 as the one they called Sir Lancelot
 when he came riding out of Britain —

— along with all the sweet and delightful course of his exploits in love and war. From that time on, this order of chivalry kept extending and spreading itself through many different parts of the world; and within it, famous and renowned for their deeds, were the mighty Amadis of Gaul with all his sons and descendants down to the fifth generation, the valiant Felixmarte of Hircania, the never-sufficiently-praised Tirante el Blanco, and — almost in our own day — we have seen and heard and spoken with the invincible knight Don Belianis of Greece. That, gentlemen, is what it means to be a knight-errant, and what I have described is the order of his chivalry. As I have already said, I, though a sinner, have taken its vows, and what those knights professed, I profess as well. And so I travel through these lonely wild places looking for adventures, resolved in my soul to set my arm and my person against the most dangerous that fortune may offer me, in aid of the weak and the needy.”

These words were enough for the travelers to satisfy themselves that Don Quixote was out of his senses, and to see the form of madness that had taken him over; and they felt the same astonishment everyone felt on first encountering it. Vivaldo, who was a very shrewd man with a lively temperament, wanted to pass the short stretch of road they said remained before reaching the mountain where the burial would take place, so he tried to give Don Quixote an opening to carry on with his absurdities. He said to him, “It seems to me, Señor Knight-errant, that your worship has chosen one of the most austere professions in the world — I would guess that even the Carthusian monks' is not so austere.”

“It may well be as austere,” our Don Quixote replied, “but whether it is as necessary to the world, I am strongly inclined to doubt. Because if the truth must be told, the soldier who carries out his captain's orders does no less than the captain who gives them. What I mean is this: churchmen, in peace and quiet, pray to Heaven for the welfare of the world, but we soldiers and knights actually put into effect what they pray for, defending it with the strength of our arms and the edge of our swords — not under shelter, but in the open air, a target for the unbearable rays of the sun in summer and the piercing frosts of winter. So we are God's ministers on earth, the arms by which his justice is carried out here. And since the business of war, and everything connected with and belonging to it, cannot be conducted without enormous sweat, toil, and effort, it follows that those who make it their profession unquestionably labor harder than those who, in calm peace and quiet, spend their time praying to God to help the weak. I am not saying — the thought doesn't even enter my head — that the knight-errant's calling is as good as the monk's in his cell. I would only conclude, from what I endure myself, that it is beyond doubt a more laborious and more battered one, hungrier and thirstier, more wretched, more ragged, and more louse-ridden; for there is no reason to doubt that the knights-errant of old endured plenty of hardship over the course of their lives. And if some of them rose by force of arms to become emperors, believe me, it cost them dearly in blood and sweat; and if those who reached that rank had not had magicians and sages to help them, they would have been completely cheated of their ambitions and disappointed in their hopes.”

“That is my opinion too,” the traveler replied, “but one thing among many others strikes me as very wrong about knights-errant: when they find themselves about to plunge into some great and dangerous adventure where there is an obvious risk of losing their lives, they never, at the moment of starting it, think of commending themselves to God, as every good Christian should do in danger like that. Instead they commend themselves to their ladies, with as much devotion as if those ladies were their gods — which seems to me to smack somewhat of paganism.”

“Sir,” Don Quixote answered, “that can on no account be left out, and any knight-errant who acted otherwise would be disgraced. It is usual and customary in knight-errantry that the knight-errant who has his lady before him as he undertakes any great feat of arms should turn his eyes toward her softly and lovingly, as if begging her with his gaze to favor and protect him in the hazardous venture he is about to attempt; and even if no one can hear him, he is bound to murmur a few words between his teeth, commending himself to her with all his heart — and of this we have countless examples in the histories. Nor should you assume from this that knights are to skip commending themselves to God, for there will be time and opportunity to do that while they are in the middle of the task.”

“Even so,” the traveler answered, “I still have a doubt. I have often read how words pass between two knights-errant, and one thing leads to another until their anger flares; they wheel their horses around, take a good run-up across the field, and then, without further ceremony, charge at each other at full speed — and in mid-gallop they commend themselves to their ladies. What usually comes of the encounter is that one of them tumbles backward over his horse's hindquarters, run clean through by his opponent's lance, and the other can only avoid falling to the ground by clinging to his horse's mane. What I don't see is how the dead man found time to commend himself to God in the middle of work as fast-moving as that. It would have been better if the words he spent commending himself to his lady mid-charge had gone instead to his duty and obligation as a Christian. Besides, I suspect that not all knights-errant even have ladies to commend themselves to — they can't all be in love.”

“That is impossible,” said Don Quixote. “I say it is impossible that there could be a knight-errant without a lady, because being in love is as natural and proper to them as having stars is to the heavens. You will certainly never find a history in which a knight-errant appears without a love affair — and for the simple reason that without one he would be considered no legitimate knight at all, but a bastard: someone who got into the fortress of knighthood not through the door, but over the wall, like a thief and a robber.”

“Still,” said the traveler, “if I remember rightly, I believe I have read that Don Galaor, brother of the valiant Amadis of Gaul, never had any particular lady to commend himself to — and yet he was no less respected for it, and was a very tough and famous knight.”

To which our Don Quixote answered, “Sir, one lone swallow does not make a summer. Besides, I happen to know that this knight was, in secret, very deeply in love; and beyond that, his habit of falling for every woman who caught his eye was a natural inclination he could not control. But in the end, it is perfectly clear that he had one lady alone whom he made mistress of his will, and to her he commended himself very often and very privately — for he prided himself on being a discreet knight.”

“Well then, if it is essential for every knight-errant to be in love,” said the traveler, “we may fairly assume that your worship is too, since you belong to the order. And unless you pride yourself on being as discreet as Don Galaor, I beg you as earnestly as I can, in the name of this whole company and in my own, to tell us the name, the homeland, the rank, and the beauty of your lady — for she will count herself fortunate if the whole world knows she is loved and served by such a knight as your worship appears to be.”

At this Don Quixote heaved a deep sigh and said, “I cannot say for certain whether my sweet enemy is pleased or not that the world should know I serve her. I can only say, in answer to what you have so courteously asked, that her name is Dulcinea; her homeland El Toboso, a village of La Mancha; her rank must be at least that of a princess, since she is my queen and lady; and her beauty is superhuman, since in her are realized all the impossible, fantastical attributes of beauty that the poets give their ladies: her hair is gold, her forehead the Elysian Fields, her eyebrows rainbows, her eyes suns, her cheeks roses, her lips coral, her teeth pearls, her neck alabaster, her bosom marble, her hands ivory, her skin white as snow — and the parts that modesty hides from view are such, I think and believe, that thoughtful reflection can only praise them, never find anything to compare them with.”
“We would like to know her lineage, her family, and her ancestry,” said Vivaldo.

To which Don Quixote replied, “She is not of the ancient Roman Curtii, Caii, or Scipios, nor of the modern Colonnas or Orsini; not of the Moncadas or Requesenes of Catalonia, nor of the Rebellas or Villanovas of Valencia; not of the Palafoxes, Nuzas, Rocabertis, Corellas, Lunas, Alagones, Urreas, Foces, or Gurreas of Aragon; not of the Cerdas, Manriques, Mendozas, or Guzmans of Castile; not of the Alencastros, Pallas, or Meneses of Portugal. She is of the line of El Toboso of La Mancha — a lineage which, though modern, can well supply a source of noble blood for the most illustrious families of the centuries to come. And let no one dispute this with me, except on the condition that Zerbino set at the foot of the trophy of Orlando's arms, where he wrote,

Let no one move these arms
 who does not dare to test his strength against Roland.”

“Although my own family is of the Cachopins of Laredo,” said the traveler, “I won't venture to compare it with that of El Toboso of La Mancha — though, to tell the truth, no such surname has ever reached my ears until now.”
“What!” said Don Quixote. “It has never reached them?”

The rest of the party rode along listening closely to this conversation between the two of them, and even the goatherds and shepherds could see how thoroughly out of his wits our Don Quixote was. Only Sancho Panza believed that everything his master said was the truth, knowing who he was and having known him since his birth. The one thing he had trouble swallowing was the business about the fair Dulcinea del Toboso, because no such name and no such princess had ever come to his attention, even though he lived so close to El Toboso. They were traveling along talking like this when they saw, coming down through a gap between two high mountains, some twenty shepherds, all dressed in sheepskins of black wool and crowned with garlands which, as it later turned out, were some of yew and some of cypress. Six of them were carrying a bier covered with a great variety of flowers and branches. Seeing this, one of the goatherds said, “Those men coming there are the bearers of Chrysostom's body, and the foot of that mountain is the place where he ordered them to bury him.” So they hurried to reach the spot, and arrived just as the bearers had set the bier on the ground and four of them, with sharp pickaxes, were digging a grave beside a hard rock. The two groups greeted each other courteously, and then Don Quixote and his companions turned to examine the bier. On it, covered with flowers, they saw a dead body dressed as a shepherd, apparently about thirty years old, showing even in death that in life he had been handsome and gallant in his bearing. Around him on the bier itself lay several books and a number of papers, some open and some folded. Those looking on, those digging the grave, and everyone else there kept a strange silence, until one of the men who had carried the body said to another, “Look carefully, Ambrosio, whether this is the place Chrysostom spoke of, since you are so anxious that everything he directed in his will be carried out to the letter.”

“This is the place,” Ambrosio answered, “for here my poor friend told me the story of his hard fortune many times over. It was here, he told me, that he first laid eyes on that mortal enemy of the human race, and here too that he first declared to her his passion — as honorable as it was devoted — and here, at last, that Marcela ended by scorning and rejecting him, bringing the tragedy of his miserable life to a close. Here, in memory of misfortunes so great, he wanted to be laid in the depths of eternal oblivion.” Then, turning to Don Quixote and the travelers, he went on, “That body, sirs, which you are looking at with compassionate eyes, housed a soul on which Heaven lavished a vast share of its riches. That is the body of Chrysostom, who was unmatched in wit, unequaled in courtesy, unapproached in graceful bearing, a phoenix in friendship, generous without limit, serious without arrogance, cheerful without vulgarity — in short, first in everything that makes up goodness, and second to none in everything that makes up misfortune. He loved deeply and was hated; he adored and was scorned; he wooed a wild beast, he pleaded with marble, he chased the wind, he cried out to the wilderness, he served ingratitude — and his reward was to become death's prey in the middle of his life, cut short by a shepherdess he was trying to immortalize in human memory. These papers you see here could prove all of that, if he had not ordered me to commit them to the fire once I had committed his body to the earth.”

“You would treat them more harshly and cruelly than their owner himself did,” said Vivaldo, “for it is neither right nor proper to carry out the will of someone whose orders fly against all reason. It would not have been reasonable for Augustus Cæsar to allow the instructions the divine Mantuan left in his will to be carried out. So, Señor Ambrosio, while you give your friend's body to the earth, you should not give his writings to oblivion. If he issued that order out of bitterness of heart, it is not right for you to obey it against all reason. On the contrary, by granting those papers life, let Marcela's cruelty live forever, to serve as a warning in ages to come for all men to flee and avoid falling into the same danger; for I and all of us who have come here already know the story of this love-struck and heartbroken friend of yours. We know your friendship, the cause of his death, and the instructions he gave at the end of his life — and from that sad story anyone can gather how great Marcela's cruelty was, how great Chrysostom's love, and how loyal your friendship, together with the end awaiting those who recklessly run down the path that insane passion opens before their eyes. Last night we heard of Chrysostom's death and that he was to be buried here, and out of curiosity and pity we turned aside from our direct road and decided to come and see with our own eyes what had so moved our compassion merely to hear of. In consideration of that compassion, and of our wish to show it if we could by offering condolence, we beg you, good Ambrosio — or at least I beg you on my own behalf — that instead of burning those papers, you let me carry some of them away.”

And without waiting for the shepherd's answer, he reached out his hand and picked up some of the papers nearest him. Seeing this, Ambrosio said, “Out of courtesy, señor, I will grant your request for the ones you have already taken — but it is pointless to expect me to give up burning the rest.”
Vivaldo, who was eager to see what the papers contained, opened one of them right away and saw that its title was “Lay of Despair.”

Hearing it, Ambrosio said, “That is the last thing the unhappy man wrote. And so you can see, señor, the state his misfortunes brought him to, read it aloud so that everyone can hear — you will have time enough for that while we wait for the grave to be dug.”
“I will do that very willingly,” said Vivaldo; and since all the bystanders were just as eager, they gathered around him, and he, reading in a loud voice, found that it went as follows.

title: Part 1, Chapter 14
paragraphs: In which the despairing verses of the dead shepherd are inserted, together with other incidents not looked for
THE LAY OF CHRYSOSTOM

Since in your cruelty you would have the merciless rigour of your tyranny proclaimed from tongue to tongue and land to land, I will compel Hell itself to lend this stricken breast of mine deep notes of woe to serve my need of fit expression. And as I struggle to give body to the tale of all I suffer and all that you have done, the dread voice shall roll forth, carrying along shreds torn from my vitals for greater pain. Listen, then — not to sweet harmony, but to a discord wrung by mad despair out of the bitterness in this breast, to ease my heart and plant a sting in yours.

The lion's roar, the savage howl of the fierce wolf, the horrid hissing of the scaly snake, the dreadful cries of monsters yet unnamed, the crow's ill-boding croak, the hollow moan of wild winds wrestling with the restless sea, the wrathful bellow of the vanquished bull, the plaintive sobbing of the widowed dove, the envied owl's sad note, the wail of woe that rises from the dreary choir of Hell — let all these mingled in one confusing sound come to aid my soul's complaint, for pain like mine demands new modes of song.

No echoes of that discord shall be heard where Father Tagus rolls, or on the banks of the olive-bordered Betis; to the rocks or in deep caverns shall my plaint be told, by a lifeless tongue in living words; or in dark valleys or on lonely shores where no foot of man and no sunbeam falls; or among the poison-breathing swarms of monsters nourished by the sluggish Nile. For though the hoarse vague echoes of my sorrows sound only in remote solitudes, your matchless cruelty and my dismal fate shall carry them to all the spacious world.

Disdain has the power to kill, and patience dies slain by suspicion, false or true; deadly is the force of jealousy; long absence makes life a dreary void; no hope of happiness can give rest to one who lives in fear of being forgotten; and death, inevitable, waits at the door. But I, by some strange miracle, live on, a prey to absence, jealousy, and disdain; racked by suspicion as by certainty; forgotten, left alone to feed my flame. And while I suffer, no ray of hope comes through the gloom to gladden me; nor do I look for any in my despair; rather, clinging to a cureless woe, I forswear all hope forever.

Can there be hope where fear lives? Would it even be wise, when the grounds for fear are far more certain? Should I shut my eyes to jealousy when it appears through a thousand wounds of the heart? Who would not throw the door open to distrust on seeing disdain unveiled and — bitter change! — all his suspicions turned into certainties, the fair truth transformed into a lie? Oh fierce tyrant of the realms of love, oh Jealousy, put chains upon these hands! And you, Disdain, bind me with your strongest cord. But, miserable as I am, triumphant over all, my sufferings drown the memory of you both.

And now I die; and since there is no hope of happiness for me in life or death, still to my fantasy I'll fondly cling. I'll say that he is wise who loves well, and that the soul most free is the one most bound in thrall to the ancient tyrant Love. I'll say that she who is my enemy possesses in that fair body a mind as fair; that her coldness is no more than I deserve; and that by virtue of the pain he sends, Love rules his kingdom with a gentle sway. Thus self-deluding, in bitter bondage, wearing out the wretched shred of life her disdain has left me, I'll give this soul and body to the winds, with no hope of a crown of bliss in store.

You, whose injustice has supplied the cause that makes me quit the weary life I loathe — as by this wounded breast you can see how willingly I become your victim — let not my death, if it be worth a tear, cloud the clear heaven of your bright eyes; I would not have you atone in any way for the crime of having made my heart your prey. Rather let your laughter ring out gaily and prove my death your festival. Fool that I am to bid you do so — I know well that your glory gains by my untimely end.

And now is the time: come, thirsting Tantalus, up from Hell's abyss; come, Sisyphus, heaving your cruel stone; come Tityus with your vulture, and Ixion with your wheel; come the sisters of the ceaseless toil. Pour all your pains into this breast of mine, and — if such tribute to despair be due — chant in your deepest tones a doleful dirge over a corpse unworthy of a shroud. Let the three-headed guardian of the gate, and all the monstrous brood of hell, join the doleful concert: a dead lover, I think, can have no fitter funeral rites.
Lay of despair, do not grieve when you depart from this sorrowing heart; my misery brings good fortune to the cause that gave you birth, so banish sadness even in the tomb.

The "Lay of Chrysostom" met with the approval of those listening, though the reader noted that it did not quite agree with what he had heard of Marcela's reserve and decorum, since Chrysostom complained in it of jealousy, suspicion, and absence — all to the prejudice of Marcela's good name and reputation. Ambrosio, who knew his friend's most secret thoughts, replied, "Señor, to clear up that doubt I should tell you that when the unhappy man wrote this lay he was away from Marcela. He had separated himself from her voluntarily, to try if absence would have its usual effect on him; and since every kind of distress and every kind of fear plagues a banished lover, imaginary jealousies and suspicions, feared as if they were true, tormented Chrysostom. So the truth of what report tells of Marcela's virtue stands unshaken, and even envy itself should not and cannot find any fault in her save that of being cruel, somewhat haughty, and very scornful."

"That is true," said Vivaldo. And he was about to read another of the papers he had saved from the fire when he was stopped by a marvellous vision — for so it seemed — that unexpectedly presented itself: on the summit of the rock where they were digging the grave, the shepherdess Marcela appeared, so beautiful that her beauty exceeded its reputation. Those who had never seen her before gazed at her in wonder and silence, and those who were used to seeing her were no less amazed. But the moment Ambrosio caught sight of her, he addressed her with open indignation:

"Have you come, by chance, cruel basilisk of these mountains, to see whether blood will flow from the wounds of this wretched man your cruelty has robbed of life? Or have you come to gloat over the cruel work of your whims, like another pitiless Nero looking down from his height upon the ruin of Rome in flames? Or to trample arrogantly upon this ill-fated corpse, as Tarquin's ungrateful daughter trampled on her father's body? Tell us quickly why you have come or what it is you want; for since I know that Chrysostom's thoughts never failed to obey you in life, I will make all these who call themselves his friends obey you too, though he be dead."

"I have come, Ambrosio, for none of the reasons you have named," replied Marcela, "but to defend myself and to show how unreasonable all those are who blame me for their own sorrow and for Chrysostom's death. So I ask all of you who are here to listen, for it will not take much time or many words to bring the truth home to people of sense. Heaven, you say, has made me beautiful — so beautiful that in spite of yourselves my beauty leads you to love me; and because you love me, you say, and even insist, that I am obliged to love you back. By the natural understanding God has given me, I know that everything beautiful attracts love; but I cannot see how, simply because a thing is loved for its beauty, that thing is obliged to love whoever loves it. Besides, the lover of beauty may himself be ugly, and ugliness being repellent, it would be very absurd to say, 'I love you because you are beautiful; you must love me, though I am ugly.' But even supposing the beauty equal on both sides, it does not follow that the inclinations must match, for not every beauty excites love — some only please the eye without winning the heart; and if every kind of beauty roused love and won the heart, the will would wander aimlessly, unable to fix on any one object, since there is an infinity of beautiful things and an infinity of inclinations to match. True love, I have been told, is indivisible, and must be freely chosen, not compelled. If that is so — and I believe it is — why do you want me to bend my will by force, for no other reason than that you say you love me? Tell me, if Heaven had made me ugly, as it has made me beautiful, could I rightly complain of you for not loving me? Remember, too, that the beauty I have was no choice of mine — Heaven gave it to me freely, without my asking or choosing. And as the viper, though it kills with its poison, is not blamed for it, since the poison is a gift of nature, so I do not deserve reproach for being beautiful. Beauty in a modest woman is like fire at a distance or a sharp sword: the one does not burn, the other does not cut anyone who does not come too near. Honour and virtue are the ornaments of the mind, without which the body, however beautiful, has no right to be called so. And if modesty is one of the virtues that especially adds grace and charm to mind and body, why should she who is loved for her beauty part with it to please someone who is striving, for his own pleasure alone, to rob her of it? I was born free, and to live in freedom I chose the solitude of the fields. In the trees of the mountains I find my society; the clear waters of the brooks are my mirrors; to the trees and waters I tell my thoughts and confide my charms. I am a fire far off, a sword laid aside. Those whom I have inspired with love by letting them see me, I have undeceived by my words; and if their longings live on hope — and I have given none to Chrysostom or to anyone else — it cannot fairly be said that I caused his death; his own obstinacy killed him rather than my cruelty. And if it is charged against me that his intentions were honourable, and that I was therefore bound to yield to them, I answer that on this very spot where his grave is now being dug, when he declared his pure intention to me, I told him that mine was to live in perpetual solitude, and that the earth alone should enjoy the fruits of my retirement and the spoils of my beauty. If, after that open warning, he chose to persist against hope and steer against the wind, what wonder that he should sink in the depths of his infatuation? Had I encouraged him, I would have been false; had I gratified him, I would have acted against my own resolve and purpose. He was warned, and persisted; he despaired without being hated. So consider whether it is reasonable that his suffering should be laid at my door. Let the one who has been deceived complain; let the one whose encouraged hopes have proved vain give way to despair; let the one I shall entice flatter himself; let the one I shall receive boast — but let no one call me cruel or murderer to whom I make no promise, on whom I practise no deception, whom I neither entice nor receive. Heaven has not so far willed that I should love by fate, and to expect me to love by choice is idle. Let this general declaration serve for each of my suitors on his own account, and let it be understood from now on that if anyone dies for me, he dies neither of jealousy nor of misery, for she who loves no one can give no one cause for jealousy, and plain honesty is not the same as scorn. Let him who calls me wild beast and basilisk leave me alone as something noxious and evil; let him who calls me ungrateful withhold his service; who calls me wayward, not seek my company; who calls me cruel, not pursue me — for this wild beast, this basilisk, this ungrateful, cruel, wayward creature has no desire whatever to seek, serve, know, or follow them. If Chrysostom's impatience and uncontrolled passion killed him, why should my modest and circumspect behaviour be blamed? If I preserve my purity in the society of the trees, why should anyone who wants me to preserve it among men seek to rob me of it? I have, as you know, wealth of my own, and I do not covet anyone else's; my taste is for freedom and I have no relish for constraint; I neither love nor hate anyone; I do not deceive this one or court that one, or trifle with one or play with another. The modest conversation of the shepherd girls of these hamlets and the care of my goats are my recreations; my desires are bounded by these mountains, and if they wander beyond, it is only to contemplate the beauty of the heavens — the steps by which the soul travels to its first home."

With these words, and without waiting for a reply, she turned and went into the thickest part of a nearby wood, leaving everyone there lost in admiration as much of her good sense as of her beauty. Some — those struck by the irresistible shafts of her bright eyes — looked ready to follow her, heedless of the plain declaration they had just heard. Seeing this, and judging it a fitting occasion to exercise his chivalry in aid of distressed maidens, Don Quixote laid his hand on the hilt of his sword and exclaimed in a loud, clear voice:

"Let no one, of whatever rank or condition, dare to follow the beautiful Marcela, on pain of incurring my fierce indignation. She has shown by clear and satisfactory arguments that she bears little or no fault for Chrysostom's death, and that she is far from yielding to the wishes of any of her lovers. For that reason, instead of being followed and persecuted, she should in justice be honoured and esteemed by all the good people of the world, since she shows that she is the only woman in it who holds to such a virtuous resolution."

Whether because of Don Quixote's threats, or because Ambrosio told them to do their final duty to their good friend, none of the shepherds moved from the spot until, having finished the grave and burned Chrysostom's papers, they laid his body in it, not without many tears from those standing by. They covered the grave with a heavy stone until the slab was ready, which Ambrosio said he intended to have made, with an epitaph to this effect:

Beneath the stone before your eyes the body of a lover lies; in life he was a shepherd swain, in death a victim to disdain. Ungrateful, cruel, coy, and fair, was she that drove him to despair, and Love hath made her his ally for spreading wide his tyranny.

They then strewed flowers and branches over the grave, and after expressing their condolences with his friend Ambrosio, they took their leave. Vivaldo and his companion did the same; and Don Quixote said goodbye to his hosts and to the travellers, who urged him to come with them to Seville, as such a convenient place for finding adventures, since they presented themselves there in every street and round every corner more often than anywhere else. Don Quixote thanked them for their advice and for their kindness, but said that for the present he could not and would not go to Seville until he had cleared all these mountains of the highwaymen and robbers that report said filled them. Seeing his good intention, the travellers were unwilling to press him further, and once more bidding him farewell, they left him and continued their journey, in the course of which they did not fail to discuss the story of Marcela and Chrysostom along with the madness of Don Quixote. He, for his part, resolved to go in search of the shepherdess Marcela and offer her all the service he could; but things did not turn out for him as he expected, as is related in the course of this veracious history, the Second Part of which ends here.

title: Part 1, Chapter 15
paragraphs: In which is related the unfortunate adventure that Don Quixote fell into when he fell out with certain heartless Yanguesans

The sage Cid Hamete Benengeli relates that as soon as Don Quixote had taken leave of his hosts and all who had been present at the burial of Chrysostom, he and his squire rode into the same wood that they had seen the shepherdess Marcela enter. After wandering through it in all directions for more than two hours in search of her without finding her, they came to a halt in a glade covered with tender grass, beside which ran a pleasant cool stream that invited and indeed compelled them to spend there the hours of midday heat, which by now was coming on heavily. Don Quixote and Sancho dismounted, and turning Rocinante and the ass loose to graze on the abundant grass, they rummaged in the saddlebags, and without any ceremony, very peacefully and sociably, master and man made their meal of what they found in them.

Sancho had not thought it worth hobbling Rocinante, sure from what he knew of the horse's staidness and chastity that all the mares in the Cordova pastures would not lead him into anything improper. Chance, however, and the devil — who is not always asleep — arranged it so that grazing in this very valley was a drove of Galician ponies belonging to some Yanguesan carriers, whose habit it was to take their midday rest with their teams in places where grass and water were plentiful; and the spot Don Quixote happened to choose suited the Yanguesans' purpose very well. So it happened that Rocinante took a fancy to amuse himself with these ponies, and dropping his usual gait and demeanour as soon as he caught their scent, he, without asking his master's leave, broke into a brisk little trot and hurried over to make his wishes known to them. They, however, evidently preferring their pasture to him, received him with their heels and teeth so effectively that they soon broke his girths and left him naked, without a saddle to cover him. Worse still, the carriers, seeing the violence he was offering their mares, came running up armed with stakes and beat him so thoroughly that they brought him to the ground sorely battered.
By this time Don Quixote and Sancho, who had watched the drubbing of Rocinante, came up panting, and Don Quixote said to Sancho:

"So far as I can see, friend Sancho, these are not knights but low-born people of mean birth: I mention it because you can lawfully help me to take proper vengeance for the insult offered to Rocinante before our eyes."
"What the devil vengeance can we take," Sancho answered, "when they are more than twenty and we are not more than two — or, indeed, perhaps not more than one and a half?"

"I count for a hundred," replied Don Quixote, and without another word he drew his sword and attacked the Yanguesans; and excited and impelled by his master's example, Sancho did the same. To begin with, Don Quixote delivered a slash at one of them that laid open the leather jerkin he wore, together with a great portion of his shoulder. The Yanguesans, seeing themselves attacked by only two men while they were so many, fell to their stakes, and driving the pair into the middle of them, began to lay on with great zeal and energy. In fact, at the second blow they brought Sancho to the ground, and Don Quixote fared no better, despite all his skill and high spirit; and fate would have it that he should fall at the feet of Rocinante, who had not yet risen — proof of how furiously stakes can pound in angry boorish hands.
Then, seeing the damage they had done, the Yanguesans with all possible haste loaded their team and continued on their way, leaving the two adventurers a sorry sight and in a sorrier mood.
Sancho was the first to come round, and finding himself close to his master he called to him in a weak and doleful voice, "Señor Don Quixote, ah, Señor Don Quixote!"
"What is it, brother Sancho?" Don Quixote answered in the same feeble, suffering tone as Sancho.

"I'd like, if it were possible," replied Sancho Panza, "for your worship to give me a couple of sips of that fiery Blas potion of yours, if you have any of it to hand; perhaps it will be as good for broken bones as it is for wounds."

"If I only had it here, wretch that I am, what more could we want?" said Don Quixote. "But I swear to you, Sancho Panza, on the faith of a knight-errant, that before two days are out, unless fortune decides otherwise, I mean to have it in my possession, or my hand will have lost its cunning."
"But in how many days does your worship think we shall have the use of our feet again?" answered Sancho Panza.

"As for myself, I cannot guess how many," said the battered knight Don Quixote; "but I take all the blame on myself, for I had no business drawing my sword against men who were not dubbed knights like me. I believe that as a punishment for breaking the laws of chivalry, the God of battles has allowed this chastisement to be administered to me. For that reason, brother Sancho, you should take note of what I am about to tell you, since it matters greatly to the welfare of both of us. When you see rabble of this sort offering us insult, you are not to wait for me to draw my sword against them, for I shall not do it at all; you draw your sword and punish them to your heart's content, and if any knights come to their aid and defence I will take care to defend you and attack them with all my might. You have already seen by a thousand signs and proofs what the might of this strong arm of mine is equal to" — so puffed up had the poor gentleman become by his victory over the stout Biscayan.

But Sancho did not approve of his master's instruction enough to let it pass without reply: "Señor, I am a man of peace, meek and quiet, and I can put up with any affront because I have a wife and children to support and bring up. So let it be a hint to your worship — since it cannot be a command — that on no account will I draw a sword either against peasant or against knight, and that here before God I forgive any insults that have been, are, or shall be offered me, by high or low, rich or poor, noble or commoner, no rank or condition whatever excepted."

To all of which his master replied, "I wish I had breath enough to speak a little more easily, and that the pain I feel in my side would ease enough to let me explain to you, Panza, the mistake you are making. Come now, sinner, suppose the wind of fortune, so far so adverse, should turn in our favour, filling the sails of our desires so that safely and without obstacle we put into port at one of those islands I have promised you — how would it be with you if, having won it, I made you lord of it? Why, you would make that almost impossible by not being a knight, and not wanting to be one, and not having the courage or the will to avenge insults or defend your lordship. For you must know that in newly conquered kingdoms and provinces the minds of the inhabitants are never so settled, nor so well-disposed to their new lord, that there is no fear of their stirring up another change to try, as they say, what chance may bring them. So it is essential that the new possessor have good sense enough to govern, and valour enough to attack and defend himself, whatever may happen."

"In what has just happened to us," answered Sancho, "I'd have been glad to have that good sense and that valour your worship speaks of. But I swear, on the faith of a poor man, that I am more fit for plasters than for arguments. See if your worship can get up, and let us help Rocinante, though he doesn't deserve it, since he was the main cause of all this thrashing. I never would have thought it of Rocinante — I took him for as virtuous a person and as quiet as myself. They are right when they say that it takes a long time to get to know people, and that nothing is sure in this life. Who would have said that, after such mighty slashes as your worship gave that unlucky knight-errant, there was coming, riding post and right at their heels, such a great storm of sticks as has fallen on our shoulders?"

"And yet yours, Sancho," Don Quixote replied, "ought to be used to such squalls. But mine, raised in soft cloth and fine linen, plainly must feel the pain of this mishap more keenly. And if I did not imagine — why do I say imagine? — know for certain that all these annoyances are very necessary parts of the calling of arms, I would lie down here and die of pure vexation."

To this the squire replied, "Señor, since these mishaps are the harvest one reaps from chivalry, tell me — do they happen very often, or do they have their own fixed times for coming round? Because it seems to me that after two such harvests we shall be no good for a third, unless God in his infinite mercy helps us."

"Know, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that the life of knights-errant is subject to a thousand dangers and reverses, and is no less within the immediate possibility of becoming kings and emperors, as experience has shown in the case of many different knights whose histories I know well. I could tell you now, if the pain would let me, of some who simply by the might of their arm rose to the high stations I have mentioned; and those same knights, both before and after, suffered various misfortunes and miseries. The valiant Amadis of Gaul found himself in the power of his mortal enemy Arcalaus the magician, who, it is positively claimed, while holding him captive gave him more than two hundred lashes with the reins of his own horse while he was tied to one of the pillars of a courtyard. And there is a certain little-known author of no small authority who says that the Knight of Phoebus, caught in a pitfall that opened under his feet in a certain castle, on falling found himself bound hand and foot in a deep pit underground, where they administered to him one of those things they call clysters, of sand and snow-water, that nearly finished him; and if he had not been rescued in that grim extremity by a sage who was a great friend of his, it would have gone very hard with the poor knight. So I can well suffer in the company of such worthy folk, for the indignities they had to suffer were greater than what we are suffering. For I want you to know, Sancho, that wounds caused by any instruments that happen by chance to be in hand inflict no indignity, and this is laid down in the law of the duel in express terms: if, for instance, a cobbler strikes another with the last he holds in his hand, although it is in fact a piece of wood, it cannot for that reason be said that the man he struck has been cudgelled. I say this so you don't imagine that because we have been drubbed in this affair we have therefore suffered any indignity, for the weapons those men carried, and pounded us with, were nothing more than their stakes, and not one of them, so far as I remember, carried rapier, sword, or dagger."

"They gave me no time to see all that much," answered Sancho, "for hardly had I laid hand on my _tizona_ when they signed the cross on my shoulders with their sticks in such style that they took the sight out of my eyes and the strength out of my feet, stretching me out where I now lie. And the question whether or not those stake-strokes were an indignity gives me no trouble, but the pain of the blows does; they'll remain as deeply imprinted on my memory as on my shoulders."
"For all that, let me tell you, brother Panza," said Don Quixote, "that there is no memory time does not put an end to, and no pain death does not remove."

"And what greater misfortune can there be," replied Panza, "than the kind that waits for time to put an end to it and death to remove it? If our mishap were one of those that are cured with a couple of plasters, it wouldn't be so bad; but I am beginning to think that all the plasters in a hospital would scarcely be enough to put us right."

"No more of that: draw strength out of weakness, Sancho, as I mean to do," returned Don Quixote, "and let us see how Rocinante is, for it seems to me that not the smallest share of this mishap has fallen to the poor beast."
"There is nothing strange in that," replied Sancho, "since he too is a knight-errant; what I do wonder at is that my donkey should have come off scot-free where we come out scotched."

"Fortune always leaves a door open in adversity, to bring relief to it," said Don Quixote; "I say so because this little beast may now make up for the lack of Rocinante, carrying me from here to some castle where I can be cured of my wounds. And I shall not count it any dishonour to be so mounted, for I remember having read how the good old Silenus, tutor and instructor of the merry god of laughter, when he entered the city of the hundred gates, rode very contentedly on a handsome ass."
"It may be true that he rode mounted as your worship says," answered Sancho, "but there is a great difference between riding mounted and being slung across like a sack of manure."

To which Don Quixote replied, "Wounds received in battle confer honour rather than take it away; so, friend Panza, say no more about it, but, as I told you before, get up as well as you can and put me on top of your beast in whatever fashion you like, and let us go from here before night comes and surprises us in these wilds."
"And yet I have heard your worship say," observed Panza, "that it is quite proper for knights-errant to sleep in wastes and deserts, and that they consider it very good fortune."

"That," said Don Quixote, "is when they cannot help it, or when they are in love. And so true is this that there have been knights who stayed two years on rocks, in sunshine and shade and all the inclemencies of heaven, without their ladies knowing anything about it. One of these was Amadis, when, under the name of Beltenebros, he settled on the Peña Pobre for — I don't know whether it was eight years or eight months, for I am not sure of the count; in any case he stayed there doing penance for some quarrel the Princess Oriana had with him. But no more of this now, Sancho, and make haste before some mishap like Rocinante's befalls the ass too."

"The very devil would be in it then," said Sancho. And letting off thirty "ohs" and sixty sighs and a hundred and twenty curses and execrations on whoever it was that had brought him there, he raised himself, stopping halfway bent like a Turkish bow, unable to bring himself fully upright; and with all his pains he saddled his ass, which had also strayed somewhat, yielding to the excessive licence of the day. He then raised up Rocinante, who, if he had had a tongue to complain with, would assuredly have outdone both Sancho and his master in lamentation.

To be brief: Sancho fixed Don Quixote on the ass and tied Rocinante along with a leading rein, and taking the ass by the halter, he proceeded more or less in the direction in which it seemed to him the high road might be. As chance was now conducting their affairs from good to better, he had not gone a short league when the road came in sight, and on it he spotted an inn, which, to his annoyance and to Don Quixote's delight, must necessarily be a castle. Sancho insisted it was an inn, his master that it was not — that it was a castle — and the dispute lasted so long that before it was settled they had reached the place. And so Sancho entered with all his team without any further argument.

title: Part 1, Chapter 16
paragraphs: Of what happened to the ingenious gentleman in the inn that he took to be a castle

The innkeeper, seeing Don Quixote slung across the ass, asked Sancho what was the matter with him. Sancho answered that it was nothing, only that he had fallen down from a rock and bruised his ribs a little. The innkeeper had a wife whose disposition was not the kind usually found in women of her profession, for she was kind-hearted by nature and felt for the sufferings of her neighbours, so she at once set about tending to Don Quixote, and made her young daughter — a very pretty girl — help her care for their guest. There was besides in the inn, as a servant, an Asturian lass with a broad face, flat back of the head, and snub nose, blind in one eye and not very sound in the other. The elegance of her shape, to be sure, made up for all her defects: she was not seven palms from head to foot, and her shoulders, which weighed down on her somewhat, made her look at the ground more than she liked. This graceful lass, then, helped the young girl, and the two of them made up a very bad bed for Don Quixote in a garret that showed every sign of having served for many years as a hayloft. In it there was also lodged a carrier whose bed was placed a little beyond our Don Quixote's, and which — though made up only of the pack-saddles and cloths of his mules — was much better than Don Quixote's. His consisted simply of four rough boards on two unsteady trestles; a mattress so thin it might have passed for a quilt, full of lumps which, if the rents had not shown them to be wool, would have felt like pebbles in hardness; two sheets of stiff buckler leather; and a coverlet whose threads anyone who chose could have counted without missing one.

On this miserable bed Don Quixote stretched himself out, and the hostess and her daughter soon covered him with plasters from head to foot, while Maritornes — for that was the Asturian's name — held the light for them. While plastering him, the hostess, noticing how full of wheals Don Quixote was in some places, remarked that they looked more like blows than the result of a fall.

It was not blows, Sancho said, but the rock had many points and projections, each of which had left its mark. "Please, señora," he added, "see if you can save some tow, since there's no shortage of someone to use it: my own loins are rather sore too."
"Then you must have fallen as well," said the hostess.
"I did not fall," said Sancho Panza, "but from the shock I got at seeing my master fall, my body aches so much that I feel as if I'd had a thousand thwacks."
"That may well be," said the young girl, "for I've often dreamed I was falling down from a tower and never coming to the ground, and when I woke I felt as weak and shaken as if I had really fallen."
"There is the point, señora," replied Sancho Panza, "that I, without dreaming at all, but being more awake than I am now, find myself with scarcely fewer wheals than my master Don Quixote."
"What is the gentleman called?" asked Maritornes the Asturian.
"Don Quixote of La Mancha," answered Sancho Panza, "and he is a knight-adventurer, and one of the best and stoutest that have been seen in the world this long while past."
"What is a knight-adventurer?" said the lass.

"Are you so new in the world as not to know?" answered Sancho Panza. "Well then, sister, you must know that a knight-adventurer is something that in two words is seen drubbed and emperor — today the most miserable and needy creature in the world, and tomorrow will have two or three crowns of kingdoms to give to his squire."
"Then how is it," said the hostess, "that belonging to so good a master as this, you don't, judging by appearances, even have so much as a county?"

"It's too soon yet," answered Sancho, "for we have only been a month on the road in quest of adventures, and so far we haven't met with anything that can be called one. But it happens that when one thing is looked for, another thing is found; and if my master Don Quixote gets well of this wound, or fall, and I am left no worse off for it, I wouldn't trade my hopes for the best title in Spain."

Don Quixote was listening very attentively to all this conversation, and sitting up in bed as best he could, he took the hostess by the hand and said to her, "Believe me, fair lady, you may count yourself fortunate in having sheltered my person in this castle of yours — a person so distinguished that, if I do not praise myself, it is only because self-praise debases, as the saying goes; but my squire will tell you who I am. I only say that I shall keep forever inscribed in my memory the service you have rendered me, so I may give you my thanks for as long as life shall last me; and would to Heaven that Love did not hold me so enthralled and subject to its laws, and to the eyes of that beautiful ingrate whose name I murmur between my teeth, so that the eyes of this lovely damsel might be the masters of my freedom."

The hostess, her daughter, and the worthy Maritornes listened in bewilderment to the words of the knight-errant, for they understood about as much as if he had been speaking Greek, though they could see that they were all meant for expressions of goodwill and courtesy. Not being used to this kind of language, they stared at him and marvelled to themselves, for he seemed to them a man of a quite different sort from those they were used to; and thanking him in tavern phrases for his civility, they left him, while the Asturian gave her attention to Sancho, who needed it no less than his master.

The carrier had made an arrangement with her for a little recreation that night, and she had given him her word that when the guests were quiet and the family asleep she would come to find him and meet his wishes with no reserve. It is said of this good lass that she never made promises of this kind without keeping them, even when made in a forest and with no witness present, for she prided herself greatly on being a lady, and held it no disgrace to be employed as servant in an inn, since she said that misfortunes and bad luck had brought her to that position. The hard, narrow, miserable, rickety bed of Don Quixote stood first in the middle of this star-lit stable, and close beside it Sancho made his — merely a rush mat and a blanket that looked more like threadbare canvas than wool. Next to these two beds was that of the carrier, made up, as has been said, of the pack-saddles and all the trappings of the two best of his mules, though he had twelve of them — sleek, plump, and in prime condition, for he was one of the rich carriers of Arévalo, according to the author of this history, who particularly mentions this carrier because he knew him very well, and is even said to have been in some degree a relation of his. Besides, Cid Hamete Benengeli was a historian of great research and accuracy in everything, as is very evident, since he would not pass over in silence the trifles already mentioned, however small and insignificant — an example which might well be followed by those grave historians who relate things so curtly and briefly that we hardly get a taste of them, all the substance of the work being left in the inkstand from carelessness, perverseness, or ignorance. A thousand blessings on the author of "Tablante de Ricamonte" and the one who wrote that other book recounting the deeds of Conde Tomillas — with what minuteness they describe everything!

To proceed: after paying a visit to his team and giving them their second feed, the carrier stretched himself on his pack-saddles and lay waiting for his conscientious Maritornes. Sancho by now was plastered up and had lain down, and though he tried to sleep, the pain in his ribs would not let him; while Don Quixote, with the pain in his, had his eyes as wide open as a hare's.

The inn was all silent, and in the whole of it there was no light except that of a lantern that hung burning in the middle of the gateway. This strange stillness, together with the thoughts always present in our knight's mind — of the incidents described at every turn in the books that were the cause of his misfortune — conjured up in his imagination as extraordinary a delusion as can well be conceived: he fancied that he had reached a famous castle (for, as has been said, every inn he lodged in was a castle to his eyes), and that the innkeeper's daughter was the daughter of the lord of the castle, who, won by his courtly bearing, had fallen in love with him and promised to come to his bed for a while that night without her parents' knowledge. Holding all this fantasy he had constructed as solid fact, he began to feel uneasy and to consider the perilous risk his virtue was about to face, and he resolved in his heart to commit no treason against his lady Dulcinea del Toboso, even if Queen Guinevere herself and the dame Quintañona should present themselves before him.

While he was taken up with these fancies, the time and the hour — an unlucky one for him — arrived for the Asturian to come. In her smock, barefoot, with her hair gathered into a fustian coif, with noiseless and cautious steps she entered the room where the three were quartered, in search of the carrier. But she had scarcely reached the door when Don Quixote noticed her, and sitting up in his bed in spite of his plasters and the pain in his ribs, he stretched out his arms to receive his beautiful damsel. The Asturian, doubled up and silent, was groping with her hands before her in search of her lover when she ran into Don Quixote's arms; he grasped her tightly by the wrist, and drawing her towards him while she dared not utter a word, made her sit down on the bed. He felt her smock, and although it was sackcloth, it seemed to him the finest, softest silk; on her wrists she wore some glass beads, but to him they had the sheen of precious Oriental pearls; her hair, somewhat resembling a horse's mane, he rated as threads of the brightest gold of Araby, whose radiance dimmed the sun himself; her breath, which no doubt smelt of yesterday's stale salad, seemed to him to diffuse a sweet aromatic fragrance from her mouth. In short, he drew her portrait in his imagination in the same features and the same style as he had read of other princesses in his books, who, smitten by love, came with all the adornments here described to see a sorely wounded knight. So great was the poor gentleman's blindness that neither touch, nor smell, nor anything else about the good lass — which would have made anyone but a carrier vomit — was enough to undeceive him. On the contrary, he was convinced he had the goddess of beauty in his arms, and holding her firmly in his grip, he went on in a low, tender voice:

"Would that I were, lovely and exalted lady, in a position to repay so great a favour as that which you, by the sight of your great beauty, have granted me. But fortune, never tired of persecuting the good, has chosen to lay me on this bed, where I lie so bruised and broken that, although my inclination would gladly comply with yours, it is impossible. Besides, to this impossibility is added another still greater: the faith I have pledged to the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, sole lady of my most secret thoughts; and were it not for that, I should not be so insensible a knight as to miss the happy opportunity which your great goodness has offered me."

Maritornes was fretting and sweating to find herself held so fast by Don Quixote, and neither understanding nor caring about the words he addressed to her, she struggled without speaking to free herself. The worthy carrier, whose unholy thoughts kept him awake, had been aware of his doxy the moment she came in the door, and was listening attentively to all that Don Quixote said. Jealous that the Asturian should have broken her word with him for another, he drew closer to Don Quixote's bed and stood still to see what would come of this talk he could not understand; but when he saw the wench struggling to get free and Don Quixote striving to hold her, not relishing the joke, he raised his arm and delivered such a terrible cuff on the lank jaws of the amorous knight that he bathed his whole mouth in blood. Not content with that, he climbed on top of his ribs and trampled all over them at a pace rather smarter than a trot. The bed, which was somewhat crazy and not very firm on its legs, unable to support the additional weight of the carrier, came crashing to the ground. At this great noise the innkeeper woke up and at once concluded that it must be some brawl of Maritornes', because after calling loudly to her he got no answer. With that suspicion he got up, lit a lamp, and hurried to the quarter where he had heard the disturbance. The wench, seeing her master coming and knowing how terrible his temper was, frightened and panic-stricken, made for the bed of Sancho Panza, who was still asleep, and crouched on it making a ball of herself.

The innkeeper came in shouting, "Where are you, strumpet? Of course this is some of your doing." At this Sancho woke up, and feeling this mass almost on top of him, fancied he had the nightmare and began throwing fisticuffs all round, a certain share of which fell on Maritornes; who, irritated by the pain and flinging modesty aside, paid back so many in return to Sancho that she woke him fully in spite of himself. He, finding himself so handled by he knew not whom, raised himself up as well as he could, grappled with Maritornes, and between the two of them began the bitterest and funniest scrimmage in the world. The carrier, however, seeing by the light of the innkeeper's candle how it was going with his ladylove, abandoned Don Quixote and ran to bring her the help she needed; and the innkeeper did the same, but with a different intention — for his was to chastise the lass, since he believed beyond doubt that she alone was the cause of all this concert. And so, as the saying is, cat to rat, rat to rope, rope to stick: the carrier pounded Sancho, Sancho the lass, she him, and the innkeeper her, and they all worked away so briskly that they didn't give themselves a moment's rest. The best of it was that the innkeeper's lamp went out, and being left in the dark, they all laid on one another in a mass so unmercifully that there was not a sound spot left where a hand might land.

It so happened that lodging in the inn that night was an officer of what they call the Old Holy Brotherhood of Toledo, who, also hearing the extraordinary noise of the conflict, seized his staff and the tin case with his warrants and made his way in the dark into the room, crying, "Hold! In the name of the Jurisdiction! Hold! In the name of the Holy Brotherhood!"

The first man he came upon was the battered Don Quixote, stretched senseless on his back upon his broken-down bed; and his hand, falling on the beard as he felt about, he continued to cry, "Help for the Jurisdiction!" But noticing that the man he had laid hold of did not move or stir, he concluded that he was dead and that those in the room were his murderers. With this suspicion he raised his voice still louder, calling out, "Shut the inn gate; see that no one goes out; they have killed a man here!" This cry startled them all, and each dropped the fight at the point at which the voice reached him. The innkeeper retreated to his room, the carrier to his pack-saddles, the lass to her crib; the unlucky Don Quixote and Sancho alone were unable to move from where they were. The officer let go Don Quixote's beard and went out to look for a light to search for and apprehend the culprits; but not finding one — for the innkeeper had purposely put out the lantern when he retreated to his room — he was forced to fall back on the hearth, where after much time and trouble he lit another lamp.

title: Part 1, Chapter 17
paragraphs: In which are recounted the innumerable troubles which the brave Don Quixote and his good squire Sancho Panza endured in the inn that, to his misfortune, he took to be a castle
