By this time Don Quixote had recovered from his swoon; and in the same tone of voice in which he had called to his squire the day before when he lay stretched out "in the vale of the stakes," he began calling to him now, "Sancho, my friend, are you asleep? Are you sleeping, friend Sancho?"
"How can I sleep, curses on it!" returned Sancho discontentedly and bitterly, "when it's plain that all the devils have been at me this night?"

"You may well believe it," answered Don Quixote, "because either I know little, or this castle is enchanted, for you must know — but what I am about to tell you, you must swear to keep secret until after my death."
"I swear it," answered Sancho.
"I say so," Don Quixote continued, "because I hate taking away anyone's good name."
"I say," replied Sancho, "that I swear to hold my tongue about it till the end of your worship's days, and God grant I may be able to let it out tomorrow."
"Do I do you such injuries, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that you would see me dead so soon?"
"It's not for that," replied Sancho, "but because I hate keeping things long, and I don't want them to grow rotten in me from over-keeping."

"At any rate," said Don Quixote, "I have more confidence in your affection and good nature; so I'd have you know that this night one of the strangest adventures I could describe befell me. To put it briefly: a little while ago the daughter of the lord of this castle came to me, and she is the most elegant and beautiful damsel that could be found in the wide world. What could I tell you of the charms of her person, of her lively wit, of other secret matters which, to preserve the loyalty I owe to my lady Dulcinea del Toboso, I shall pass over unmentioned and in silence! I will only tell you that, either fate being envious of so great a boon placed in my hands by good fortune, or perhaps — and this is more likely — this castle being, as I've already said, enchanted, at the very moment when I was engaged in the sweetest and most amorous talk with her, without my seeing or knowing where it came from there came a hand attached to the arm of some huge giant, and it planted such a cuff on my jaws that they are all bathed in blood. Then it pummelled me in such a way that I'm in worse shape than yesterday when the carriers, on account of Rocinante's misbehaviour, inflicted on us the injury you know of. So I conclude there must be some enchanted Moor guarding the treasure of this damsel's beauty, and that it isn't reserved for me."

"Not for me either," said Sancho, "for more than four hundred Moors have so thrashed me that the drubbing of the stakes was cakes and fancy-bread compared to it. But tell me, señor, what do you call this excellent, rare adventure that has left us as we are now? Your worship wasn't so badly off, having in your arms that incomparable beauty you spoke of; but I, what did I have, except the heaviest whacks I think I've ever had in all my life? Unlucky me, and the mother who bore me! I'm not a knight-errant and never expect to be one, and the greater part of every misfortune falls to my share."
"Then you have been thrashed too?" said Don Quixote.
"Didn't I just say so? Worse luck to my line!" said Sancho.
"Don't be distressed, friend," said Don Quixote, "for I will now make the precious balsam with which we shall cure ourselves in the twinkling of an eye."

By this time the officer had succeeded in lighting the lamp, and came in to see the man he thought had been killed. When Sancho caught sight of him at the door — in his shirt, with a cloth on his head and a lamp in his hand, and a very forbidding face — he said to his master, "Señor, can this be the enchanted Moor come back to give us more punishment, if there's anything still left in the ink-bottle?"
"It cannot be the Moor," answered Don Quixote, "for those under enchantment do not let themselves be seen by anyone."
"If they don't let themselves be seen, they let themselves be felt," said Sancho; "if not, let my shoulders speak to the point."
"Mine could speak too," said Don Quixote, "but that's not enough reason to believe that what we see is the enchanted Moor."

The officer came up, and finding them engaged in such a peaceful conversation, stood amazed; though Don Quixote, to be sure, still lay on his back unable to move from sheer pummelling and plasters. The officer turned to him and said, "Well, how goes it, my good man?"
"I'd speak more politely if I were you," replied Don Quixote; "is it the way of this country to address knights-errant in that style, you booby?"

The officer, finding himself so disrespectfully treated by such a sorry-looking individual, lost his temper, and raising the lamp full of oil, struck Don Quixote such a blow on the head with it that he gave him a badly broken pate. Then, everything being in darkness, he went out, and Sancho Panza said, "That is certainly the enchanted Moor, señor, and he keeps the treasure for others, and for us only the cuffs and the lamp-whacks."

"That is the truth," answered Don Quixote, "and there is no point in troubling oneself about these matters of enchantment, or in being angry or vexed at them — for since they are invisible and visionary, we shall find no one to take vengeance on, do what we may. Get up, Sancho, if you can, and call the alcaide of this fortress, and get him to give me a little oil, wine, salt, and rosemary to make the salutiferous balsam; for indeed I think I have great need of it now, since I am losing much blood from the wound that phantom gave me."

Sancho got up with pain enough in his bones, and went after the innkeeper in the dark. Meeting the officer, who was looking to see what had become of his enemy, he said to him, "Señor, whoever you are, do us the favour and kindness of giving us a little rosemary, oil, salt, and wine, which are needed to cure one of the best knights-errant on earth, who lies on yonder bed wounded by the hands of the enchanted Moor that is in this inn."

When the officer heard him talk this way, he took him for a man out of his senses; and as day was now beginning to break, he opened the inn gate and, calling the host, told him what this good man wanted. The host furnished him with what he asked for, and Sancho brought it to Don Quixote, who, with his hand to his head, was bewailing the pain of the blow of the lamp — which had done him no more harm than to raise a couple of rather large lumps; and what he fancied was blood was only the sweat that flowed from him in his sufferings during the late storm. To be brief, he took the materials, mixed them all and boiled them a good while, until it seemed to him they had come to perfection. He then asked for some vial to pour it into, and as there was not one in the inn, he decided on putting it into a tin oil-bottle or flask the host gave him as a free gift; and over the flask he repeated more than eighty paternosters and as many more ave-marias, salves, and credos, accompanying each word with a cross by way of benediction. Sancho, the innkeeper, and the officer were all present, for the carrier was by now peacefully occupied in attending to the comfort of his mules.

This accomplished, he felt eager to test the virtue of this precious balsam on the spot, as he considered it, and so he drank nearly a quart of what could not be put into the flask and remained in the pigskin in which it had been boiled. But scarcely had he done drinking when he began to vomit so violently that nothing was left in his stomach; and with the pangs and spasms of vomiting he broke into a profuse sweat, on account of which he asked them to cover him up and leave him alone. They did so, and he lay sleeping more than three hours, at the end of which he woke and felt very great bodily relief and so much ease from his bruises that he thought himself quite cured, and truly believed he had hit upon the balsam of Fierabras; and that with this remedy he might from then on, without any fear, face any kind of destruction, battle, or combat, however perilous.

Sancho Panza, who also regarded his master's recovery as miraculous, begged him to give him what was left in the pigskin, which was no small quantity. Don Quixote consented, and Sancho, taking it with both hands, in good faith and with even better will, gulped down and drained off very little less than his master. But the fact is, poor Sancho's stomach was of necessity not so delicate as that of his master, so before vomiting he was seized with such gripings and retchings, and such sweats and faintness, that he truly believed his last hour had come; and finding himself so racked and tormented, he cursed the balsam and the thief who had given it to him.

Don Quixote, seeing him in this state, said, "It is my belief, Sancho, that this mischief comes of your not being dubbed a knight, for I am convinced this liquor cannot be good for those who are not."
"If your worship knew that," returned Sancho — "woe betide me and all my kindred! — why did you let me taste it?"

At that moment the draught took effect, and the poor squire began to discharge both ways at such a rate that the rush mat he had thrown himself on, and the canvas blanket covering him, were fit for nothing afterwards. He sweated and convulsed with such paroxysms that not only he himself but everyone present thought his end had come. This tempest and tribulation lasted about two hours, at the end of which he was left — not like his master, but so weak and exhausted that he could not stand. Don Quixote, however, who, as has been said, felt himself relieved and well, was eager to take his departure at once in quest of adventures, since it seemed to him that all the time he lingered there was a fraud upon the world and on those in it who stood in need of his help and protection — all the more so now that he had the security and confidence his balsam gave him. Urged by this impulse, he saddled Rocinante himself and put the pack-saddle on his squire's beast, whom he likewise helped to dress and mount. Then he mounted his horse, and turning to a corner of the inn he laid hold of a pike that stood there, to serve him as a lance. Everyone in the inn — more than twenty people — stood watching him; the innkeeper's daughter was also watching him, and he too never took his eyes off her, and from time to time fetched a sigh that he seemed to pluck up from the depths of his bowels; but they all assumed it was from the pain in his ribs — at any rate those who had seen him plastered the night before thought so.

As soon as they were both mounted at the gate of the inn, he called to the host and said in a very grave and measured voice, "Many and great are the favours, Señor Alcaide, that I have received in this castle of yours, and I remain under the deepest obligation to be grateful to you for them all the days of my life. If I can repay them by avenging you of any arrogant foe who may have wronged you, know that my calling is no other than to aid the weak, to avenge those who suffer wrong, and to chastise treachery. Search your memory, and if you find anything of the kind, you need only tell me of it, and I promise you, by the order of knighthood I have received, to procure you satisfaction and reparation to the utmost of your wishes."

The innkeeper replied with equal calmness, "Sir knight, I do not want your worship to avenge me of any wrong, because when any is done me I can take what vengeance seems good to me; the only thing I want is that you pay me the bill you have run up in the inn last night — for the straw and barley for your two beasts, as well as for supper and beds."
"Then this is an inn?" said Don Quixote.
"And a very respectable one," said the innkeeper.

"I have been mistaken all this time," answered Don Quixote, "for in truth I thought it was a castle, and not a bad one; but since it appears it is not a castle but an inn, all that can be done now is for you to waive the payment, for I cannot contravene the rule of knights-errant — and I know for a fact, having read nothing to the contrary, that they never paid for lodging or anything else at the inn where they happened to be. Any hospitality offered them is their due by law and right, in return for the unbearable toil they endure in seeking adventures by night and by day, in summer and in winter, on foot and on horseback, in hunger and thirst, cold and heat, exposed to all the inclemencies of heaven and the hardships of earth."
"I have little to do with that," replied the innkeeper; "pay me what you owe me, and let's have no more talk of chivalry, for all I care about is getting my money."

"You are a stupid, scurvy innkeeper," said Don Quixote; and putting spurs to Rocinante and bringing his pike to the slope, he rode out of the inn before anyone could stop him, and pushed on some distance without looking back to see if his squire was following.

The innkeeper, seeing him go without paying, ran to collect from Sancho, who said that since his master would not pay, neither would he, because, being squire to a knight-errant, the same rule and reasoning applied to him as to his master about not paying anything at inns and hostelries. At this the innkeeper grew very angry, and threatened, if he did not pay, to compel him in a way he would not like. To which Sancho answered that by the law of chivalry his master had received, he would not pay a single coin even if it cost him his life; for the excellent and ancient custom of knights-errant was not going to be violated by him, nor should the squires of those yet to come into the world ever complain of him, or reproach him for breaking so just a privilege.

The ill-luck of unfortunate Sancho so ordered things that among the company in the inn there were four wool-carders from Segovia, three needle-makers from the Colt of Cordova, and two lodgers from the Fair of Seville — lively fellows, tender-hearted, fond of a joke, and playful. Almost as if instigated and moved by a common impulse, they made up to Sancho and pulled him off his ass; one of them went in to fetch the blanket from the host's bed. But on flinging him into it they looked up, and seeing that the ceiling was somewhat lower than they needed for their work, they decided to go out into the yard, which was bounded by the sky, and there, placing Sancho in the middle of the blanket, they began to toss him high in the air, having sport with him as they would with a dog at Shrovetide.

The cries of the poor blanketed wretch were so loud that they reached the ears of his master, who, halting to listen attentively, was persuaded that some new adventure was at hand, until he clearly recognised that it was his squire calling out. Wheeling about, he came up to the inn at a laborious gallop, and finding it shut, went round it to see if he could find some way of getting in. But as soon as he came to the wall of the yard, which was not very high, he discovered the game being played with his squire. He saw him rising and falling in the air with such grace and nimbleness that, had his rage allowed him, it is my belief he would have laughed. He tried to climb from his horse onto the top of the wall, but he was so bruised and battered he could not even dismount; and so, from the back of his horse, he began to hurl such curses and abuses at those blanketing Sancho as it would be impossible to write down accurately. They, however, did not stop their laughter or their work for that, nor did the flying Sancho stop his lamentations, mingled now with threats, now with entreaties, but all to little purpose, or none at all, until from sheer weariness they left off. They then brought him his ass, and mounting him on top of it, they put his jacket round him; and the compassionate Maritornes, seeing him so exhausted, thought fit to refresh him with a jug of water, and that it might be all the cooler she fetched it from the well. Sancho took it, and as he was raising it to his mouth he was stopped by the cries of his master exclaiming, "Sancho, my son, drink no water; do not drink it, my son, for it will kill you; see, here I have the blessed balsam" — and he held up the flask of liquor — "and with two drops of it you will certainly be restored."

At these words Sancho turned his eyes sideways, and in an even louder voice said, "Has your worship forgotten that I am not a knight, or do you want me to end by vomiting up what bowels I have left after last night? Keep your liquor, in the name of all the devils, and leave me to myself!" And at one and the same instant he stopped talking and began drinking; but as at the first sip he noticed it was water, he did not care to go on with it, and begged Maritornes to fetch him some wine, which she did with right good will, paying for it with her own money — for indeed it was said of her that, though she was in that line of life, there was some faint and distant resemblance to a Christian about her. When Sancho had done drinking he dug his heels into his ass, and the gate of the inn being thrown open, he passed out very well pleased at having paid nothing and carried his point, though it had been at the expense of his usual sureties, his shoulders. It is true the innkeeper kept his saddlebags in payment of what was owed; but Sancho took his departure in such a flurry that he never missed them. The innkeeper, as soon as he saw him off, wanted to bar the gate close, but the blanketers would not agree to it, for they were fellows who would not have cared two farthings for Don Quixote, even if he had really been one of the knights-errant of the Round Table.

title: Part 1, Chapter 18
paragraphs: In which is related the conversation Sancho Panza held with his master, Don Quixote, and other adventures worth relating

Sancho reached his master so limp and faint that he could not urge on his beast. When Don Quixote saw the state he was in, he said, "I have now come to the conclusion, good Sancho, that this castle or inn is beyond a doubt enchanted; for those who so atrociously amused themselves with you — what can they be but phantoms or beings of another world? I take this as confirmed by having noticed that when I was at the wall of the yard witnessing the acts of your sad tragedy, it was out of my power to climb up onto it, nor could I even dismount from Rocinante, because they no doubt had me enchanted. I swear to you by the faith of what I am, that if I had been able to climb up or dismount, I would have avenged you in such a way that those braggart thieves would have remembered their freak forever, even though in doing so I should have broken the laws of chivalry, which, as I have often told you, do not permit a knight to lay hands on one who is not, except in case of urgent and great necessity in defence of his own life and person."

"I would have avenged myself too if I could," said Sancho, "whether I had been dubbed knight or not — but I could not. Though for my part I am convinced those who amused themselves with me were not phantoms or enchanted men, as your worship says, but men of flesh and bone like ourselves. They all had names — I heard them call each other when they were tossing me; one was called Pedro Martinez, another Tenorio Hernandez, and the innkeeper, I heard, was called Juan Palomeque the Left-handed. So, señor, your not being able to leap over the wall of the yard or dismount from your horse was due to something other than enchantments. What I make of all this clearly is that the adventures we go seeking will in the end lead us into such misadventures that we won't know which is our right foot; and the best and wisest thing, in my small judgement, would be for us to return home, now that it is harvest time, and attend to our business, and give over wandering from Zeca to Mecca and from pail to bucket, as the saying is."

"How little you know about chivalry, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "hold your peace and be patient. The day will come when you shall see with your own eyes what an honourable thing it is to wander in the pursuit of this calling. Tell me, what greater pleasure can there be in the world, or what delight can equal that of winning a battle and triumphing over one's enemy? None, beyond all doubt."

"Very likely," answered Sancho, "though I do not know it. All I know is that since we have been knights-errant — or since your worship has been one (for I have no right to count myself one of so honourable a number) — we have never won any battle except the one with the Biscayan, and even out of that your worship came with half an ear and half a helmet the less. From then till now it has been all cudgellings and more cudgellings, cuffs and more cuffs, I getting the blanketing on top of it all, and falling in with enchanted persons on whom I can't avenge myself so as to know what the delight of conquering an enemy is like, as your worship calls it."

"That is what vexes me, and what ought to vex you, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "but from now on I will endeavour to have at hand some sword made with such craft that no kind of enchantment can take effect on him who carries it. It is even possible that fortune may procure for me the one that belonged to Amadis when he was called 'The Knight of the Burning Sword' — one of the best swords any knight in the world ever possessed; for besides having that virtue, it cut like a razor, and there was no armour, however strong and enchanted, that could resist it."

"Such is my luck," said Sancho, "that even if that happened and your worship found such a sword, it would, like the balsam, turn out to be useful and good only for dubbed knights, and as for the squires, they might sup sorrow."
"Fear not that, Sancho," said Don Quixote: "Heaven will deal better by you."

Talking like this, Don Quixote and his squire were going along when, on the road they were following, Don Quixote saw approaching them a large and thick cloud of dust; on seeing which he turned to Sancho and said:

"This is the day, Sancho, on which will be seen the boon my fortune is reserving for me; this, I say, is the day on which, as much as on any other, the might of my arm will be displayed, and on which I shall do deeds that shall remain written in the book of fame for all ages to come. Do you see that cloud of dust rising yonder? Well then, it is being churned up by a vast army composed of various and countless nations marching there."
"In that case there must be two," said Sancho, "for on the opposite side here there rises just such another cloud of dust."

Don Quixote turned to look and found it was true. Rejoicing greatly, he concluded that they were two armies about to engage and clash in the middle of that broad plain; for at all times and seasons his imagination was full of the battles, enchantments, adventures, crazy feats, loves, and defiances recorded in the books of chivalry, and everything he said, thought, or did had reference to such things. Now the cloud of dust he had seen was raised by two great droves of sheep coming along the same road in opposite directions, which, because of the dust, did not become visible until they drew near. But Don Quixote insisted so positively that they were armies that Sancho was led to believe it, and said, "Well, what are we to do, señor?"

"What?" said Don Quixote; "give aid and assistance to the weak and those in need. You must know, Sancho, that the army coming towards us is led and commanded by the mighty emperor Alifanfaron, lord of the great island of Trapobana; the other that marches behind me is that of his enemy, the king of the Garamantas, Pentapolin of the Bare Arm — so called because he always goes into battle with his right arm bare."
"But why are these two lords such enemies?"

"They are at enmity," replied Don Quixote, "because this Alifanfaron is a furious pagan and is in love with the daughter of Pentapolin, who is a very beautiful and gracious lady, and a Christian; and her father refuses to give her to the pagan king unless he first abandons the religion of his false prophet Mahomet and adopts his own."
"By my beard," said Sancho, "Pentapolin is quite right, and I'll help him all I can."
"In that you will do what is your duty, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "for to engage in battles of this sort there is no requirement of being a dubbed knight."

"That I can well understand," answered Sancho; "but where shall we put this ass to be sure of finding him again after the fray is over? Because I don't believe it has been the custom so far to go into battle on a beast of this kind."

"That is true," said Don Quixote, "and the best thing you can do with him is to leave him to his fate, whether he be lost or not, for we shall have so many horses when we come out victorious that even Rocinante runs a risk of being exchanged for another. But pay attention and observe, for I want to give you some account of the chief knights in these two armies; and so that you may see and mark them better, let us withdraw to that hillock rising yonder, from which both armies can be seen."

They did so, and placed themselves on a rising ground from which the two droves that Don Quixote made armies of might have been plainly seen, if the clouds of dust they raised had not obscured and blinded the sight. Nevertheless, seeing in his imagination what he did not see and what did not exist, he began in a loud voice:

"That knight you see yonder in yellow armour, who bears on his shield a lion crowned crouching at the feet of a damsel, is the valiant Laurcalco, lord of the Silver Bridge; that one in armour with flowers of gold, who bears on his shield three crowns argent on an azure field, is the dreaded Micocolembo, grand duke of Quirocia; that other of giant frame, on his right hand, is the ever-dauntless Brandabarbaran de Boliche, lord of the three Arabias, who for armour wears that serpent skin and has for shield a gate which, according to tradition, is one of those of the temple Samson brought to the ground when by his death he revenged himself on his enemies. But turn your eyes to the other side and you shall see, in the front and vanguard of this other army, the ever-victorious and never-vanquished Timonel of Carcajona, prince of New Biscay, who comes in armour with arms quartered azure, vert, white, and yellow, and bears on his shield a cat or on a field tawny with a motto that says _Miau_, which is the beginning of the name of his lady, who according to report is the peerless Miaulina, daughter of the duke Alfeniquen of the Algarve. The other, who burdens and presses the loins of that powerful charger and bears arms white as snow and a shield blank and without any device, is a novice knight, a Frenchman by birth, Pierres Papin by name, lord of the baronies of Utrique. That other, who with iron-shod heels strikes the flanks of that nimble parti-coloured zebra, and for arms bears azure vair, is the mighty duke of Nerbia, Espartafilardo del Bosque, who bears for device on his shield an asparagus plant with a motto in Castilian that says, _'Rastrea mi suerte'_." And so he went on naming a great many knights of one squadron or the other out of his imagination, and to all he assigned off the cuff their arms, colours, devices, and mottoes, carried away by the illusions of his unheard-of mania. Without a pause, he continued, "The people of various nations compose this squadron in front: here are those who drink from the sweet waters of the famous Xanthus; those who scour the wooded Massilian plains; those who sift the pure fine gold of Arabia Felix; those who enjoy the famed cool banks of the crystal Thermodon; those who in many and various ways divert the streams of the golden Pactolus; the Numidians, faithless in their promises; the Persians renowned in archery; the Parthians and the Medes who fight as they fly; the Arabs who are forever shifting their dwellings; the Scythians as cruel as they are fair; the Ethiopians with pierced lips; and an infinity of other nations whose features I recognise, though I cannot recall their names. In this other squadron come those who drink the crystal streams of the olive-bearing Betis; those who smooth their faces with the water of the ever-rich and golden Tagus; those who rejoice in the fertilising flow of the divine Genil; those who roam the Tartesian plains abounding in pasture; those who take their pleasure in the Elysian meadows of Jerez; the rich Manchegans crowned with ruddy ears of corn; the wearers of iron, old relics of the Gothic race; those who bathe in the Pisuerga renowned for its gentle current; those who feed their herds along the spreading pastures of the winding Guadiana, famed for its hidden course; those who tremble with the cold of the pine-clad Pyrenees or the dazzling snows of the lofty Apennine — in a word, as many as all Europe includes and contains."

Good God! What a number of countries and nations he named! Giving to each its proper attributes with marvellous readiness — brimful and saturated with what he had read in his lying books! Sancho Panza hung on his words without speaking, and from time to time turned to try if he could see the knights and giants his master was describing; and as he could not make out a single one of them he said:
"Señor, devil take it if there's a sign of any man you talk of, knight or giant, in the whole thing; maybe it's all enchantment, like the phantoms last night."
"How can you say that!" answered Don Quixote; "don't you hear the neighing of the steeds, the braying of the trumpets, the roll of the drums?"
"I hear nothing but a great bleating of ewes and sheep," said Sancho; which was true, for by this time the two flocks had come close.

"The fear you are in, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "prevents you from seeing or hearing correctly, for one of the effects of fear is to derange the senses and make things appear different from what they are. If you are in such fear, withdraw to one side and leave me to myself, for alone I am enough to bring victory to the side I give my aid to." So saying, he gave Rocinante the spur, and putting his lance in rest, shot down the slope like a thunderbolt. Sancho shouted after him, "Come back, Señor Don Quixote; I vow to God they are sheep and ewes you are charging! Come back! Unlucky the father that begot me! What madness is this? Look, there is no giant, nor knight, nor cats, nor arms, nor shields quartered or whole, nor vair azure or bedevilled. What are you doing? Sinner that I am before God!" But not for all these entreaties did Don Quixote turn back; on the contrary, he went on shouting, "Ho, knights, you who follow and fight under the banners of the valiant emperor Pentapolin of the Bare Arm, follow me all of you; you shall see how easily I shall give him his revenge over his enemy Alifanfaron of the Trapobana."

So saying, he dashed into the middle of the squadron of ewes, and began to spear them with as much spirit and intrepidity as if he were transfixing mortal enemies in earnest. The shepherds and drovers accompanying the flock shouted at him to stop; seeing it was no use, they ungirt their slings and began to salute his ears with stones as big as a fist. Don Quixote paid no heed to the stones, but, letting drive right and left, kept saying:

"Where are you, proud Alifanfaron? Come before me; I am a single knight who wants to test your prowess hand to hand, and make you yield your life as a penalty for the wrong you do to the valiant Pentapolin Garamanta." Here came a sugar-plum from the brook that struck him on the side and buried a couple of ribs in his body. Feeling himself so smitten, he imagined himself slain or badly wounded for certain, and remembering his liquor he drew out his flask, put it to his mouth, and began to pour the contents into his stomach; but before he had managed to swallow what seemed to him enough, another almond came that struck him on the hand and on the flask so fairly that it smashed the flask to pieces, knocking three or four teeth and grinders out of his mouth in the process, and badly crushing two fingers of his hand. Such was the force of the first blow and of the second that the poor knight, in spite of himself, came down backwards off his horse. The shepherds came up, and felt sure they had killed him; so in all haste they collected their flock together, took up the dead beasts — of which there were more than seven — and made off without waiting to find out anything further.

All this time Sancho stood on the hill watching the crazy feats his master was performing, and tearing his beard and cursing the hour and occasion when fortune had made him acquainted with him. Seeing him then brought to the ground, and that the shepherds had taken themselves off, he ran to him and found him in a very bad way, though not unconscious; and said:
"Didn't I tell you to come back, Señor Don Quixote, and that what you were going to attack were not armies but droves of sheep?"

"That's how that thief of a sage, my enemy, can alter and falsify things," answered Don Quixote; "you must know, Sancho, that it is a very easy matter for people of his sort to make us believe whatever they choose; and this malignant being who persecutes me, envious of the glory he knew I was to win in this battle, has turned the enemy squadrons into droves of sheep. At any rate, do this much, I beg of you, Sancho — to undeceive yourself, and see that what I say is true: mount your ass and follow them quietly, and you'll see that when they have gone some little way from here they will return to their original shape and, ceasing to be sheep, become men in all respects as I described them to you at first. But don't go just yet, for I need your help and assistance. Come here, and see how many of my teeth and grinders are missing, for I feel as if there isn't one left in my mouth."

Sancho came so close that he almost put his eyes into his mouth; and just at that moment the balsam was acting on Don Quixote's stomach, so at the very instant when Sancho came to examine his mouth, he discharged all its contents with more force than a musket, full into the beard of the compassionate squire.

"Holy Mary!" cried Sancho, "what is this that has happened to me? Clearly this sinner is mortally wounded, since he vomits blood from his mouth"; but considering the matter a little more closely, he perceived by the colour, taste, and smell that it was not blood but the balsam from the flask he had seen him drink. And he was taken with such a loathing that his stomach turned, and he vomited up his insides over his very master, and both were left in a precious state. Sancho ran to his ass to get something out of his saddlebags to clean himself and relieve his master; but not finding them, he nearly took leave of his senses, cursed himself anew, and resolved in his heart to quit his master and return home, even if he forfeited the wages of his service and all hopes of the promised island.

Don Quixote now rose, and putting his left hand to his mouth to keep his teeth from falling out altogether, with the other he laid hold of Rocinante's bridle — the horse had never stirred from his master's side, so loyal and well-behaved was he — and went over to where the squire stood leaning over his ass with his hand to his cheek, like a man in deep dejection. Seeing him in this mood, looking so sad, Don Quixote said:

"Bear in mind, Sancho, that one man is no more than another, unless he does more than another. All these tempests that fall upon us are signs that fair weather is coming shortly, and that things will go well with us, for it is impossible for good or evil to last forever; and so it follows that, the evil having lasted long, the good must be now close at hand. So you must not distress yourself at the misfortunes that happen to me, since you have no share in them."

"How have I not?" replied Sancho. "Was the one they blanketed yesterday perhaps anyone other than my father's son? And the saddlebags that are missing today with all my treasures — did they belong to anyone but me?"
"What! The saddlebags are missing, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.
"Yes, they are missing," answered Sancho.
"In that case we have nothing to eat today," replied Don Quixote.

"It would be so," answered Sancho, "if there were none of those herbs your worship says you know about in these meadows — the ones with which knights-errant as unlucky as your worship are accustomed to make up for such shortcomings."

"For all that," answered Don Quixote, "I would rather have right now a quarter of bread, or a loaf and a couple of pilchards' heads, than all the herbs described by Dioscorides, even with Doctor Laguna's notes. Nevertheless, Sancho the Good, mount your beast and come along with me; God, who provides for all things, will not fail us — especially when we are so active in his service as we are — since he fails not the midges of the air, nor the grubs of the earth, nor the tadpoles of the water, and is so merciful that he maketh his sun to rise on the good and on the evil, and sendeth rain on the unjust and on the just."
"Your worship would make a better preacher than knight-errant," said Sancho.

"Knights-errant knew and ought to know everything, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "for there were knights-errant in former times as well qualified to deliver a sermon or discourse in the middle of an encampment as if they had taken a degree at the University of Paris; whereby we may see that the lance has never blunted the pen, nor the pen the lance."

"Well, be it as your worship says," replied Sancho; "let us be off now and find some place of shelter for the night, and God grant it may be somewhere where there are no blankets, nor blanketeers, nor phantoms, nor enchanted Moors; for if there are, may the devil take the whole concern."

"Ask that of God, my son," said Don Quixote; "and lead on wherever you like, for this time I leave our lodging to your choice. But reach me your hand, and feel with your finger, and tell me how many teeth and grinders are missing from this right side of my upper jaw, for that is where I feel the pain."
Sancho put in his fingers, and feeling about, asked him, "How many grinders did your worship have on this side?"
"Four," replied Don Quixote, "besides the back-tooth, all whole and quite sound."
"Mind what you are saying, señor."
"I say four, if not five," answered Don Quixote, "for never in my life have I had a tooth or grinder drawn, nor has any fallen out or been destroyed by decay or rheum."
"Well, then," said Sancho, "on this lower side your worship has no more than two grinders and a half, and on the upper neither a half nor any at all — it's all as smooth as the palm of my hand."

"Luckless that I am!" said Don Quixote, hearing the sad news his squire gave him. "I had rather they had stripped me of an arm, so long as it were not my sword-arm; for I tell you, Sancho, a mouth without teeth is like a mill without a millstone, and a tooth is much more to be prized than a diamond. But we who profess the austere order of chivalry are liable to all this. Mount, friend, and lead the way, and I will follow you at whatever pace you wish."

Sancho did as he was told, and proceeded in the direction in which he thought he might find shelter without leaving the high road, which was very much frequented there. As they went along at a slow pace — for the pain in Don Quixote's jaws kept him uneasy and not in the mood for speed — Sancho thought it well to amuse and divert him with talk of some kind, and among the things he said to him was what will be told in the following chapter.

title: Part 1, Chapter 19
paragraphs: Of the shrewd conversation Sancho held with his master, and of the adventure that befell him with a dead body, together with other notable occurrences

"It seems to me, señor, that all these mishaps that have befallen us of late have undoubtedly been a punishment for the offence committed by your worship against the order of chivalry, in not keeping the oath you made not to eat bread off a tablecloth or embrace the queen, and all the rest of it that your worship swore to observe until you had taken that helmet of Malandrino's, or whatever the Moor is called — for I don't quite remember."

"You are quite right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "but to tell the truth it had escaped my memory; and likewise you may rely upon it that the business of the blanket happened to you because of your fault in not reminding me of it in time. But I will make amends, for there are ways of compounding for everything in the order of chivalry."
"Why! Have I taken an oath of some sort, then?" said Sancho.

"It makes no difference that you have not taken an oath," said Don Quixote; "it is enough that I see you are not quite clear of complicity; and whether or not, it will not be ill done to provide ourselves with a remedy."

"In that case," said Sancho, "mind that your worship does not forget this as you did the oath; perhaps the phantoms may take it into their heads to amuse themselves once more with me; or even with your worship, if they see you so obstinate."

While they were engaged in this and other talk, night overtook them on the road before they had reached or come in sight of any place of shelter; and what made it still worse was that they were dying of hunger, since with the loss of the saddlebags they had lost their entire larder and commissariat. To complete the misfortune, they met with an adventure that, without any invention, really had the appearance of one. It happened that the night closed in somewhat darkly, but for all that they pushed on, Sancho feeling sure that since the road was the king's highway they might reasonably expect to find some inn within a league or two. Going along like this — the night dark, the squire hungry, the master sharp-set — they saw coming towards them on the road they were travelling a great number of lights that looked exactly like stars in motion. Sancho was taken aback at the sight, and Don Quixote did not altogether relish them: the one pulled up his ass by the halter, the other his hack by the bridle, and they stood still, watching anxiously to see what all this would turn out to be; and they found that the lights were approaching them, and the nearer they came the larger they seemed. At this spectacle Sancho began to shake like a man dosed with mercury, and Don Quixote's hair stood on end; but plucking up a little spirit, he said:
"This, no doubt, Sancho, will be a most mighty and perilous adventure, in which it will be necessary for me to put forth all my valour and resolution."
"Unlucky me!" answered Sancho. "If this adventure happens to be one of phantoms, as I'm beginning to think it is, where shall I find the ribs to bear it?"

"Be they phantoms ever so much," said Don Quixote, "I will not let them touch a thread of your garments; for if they played tricks with you the time before, it was because I was unable to leap the walls of the yard. But now we are on a wide plain, where I shall be able to wield my sword as I please."
"And if they enchant and cripple you as they did the last time," said Sancho, "what difference will it make being on the open plain or not?"
"For all that," replied Don Quixote, "I entreat you, Sancho, to keep a good heart, for experience will tell you what mine is."

"I will, please God," answered Sancho. And the two, withdrawing to one side of the road, set themselves to observe closely what all these moving lights might be; and very soon afterwards they made out some twenty figures in white robes, all on horseback with lighted torches in their hands, the awe-inspiring aspect of which completely extinguished Sancho's courage; he began to chatter his teeth like a man in the cold fit of an ague. His heart sank and his teeth chattered still more when they saw distinctly that behind them came a litter covered with black, followed by six more mounted figures in mourning down to the very feet of their mules — for they could see plainly they were not horses by the easy pace at which they went. As the white-robed riders came along they muttered to themselves in low, plaintive tones. This strange spectacle at such an hour and in such a solitary place was quite enough to strike terror into Sancho's heart, and even into his master's; and (except in Don Quixote's case) it did so, for all of Sancho's resolution had now broken down. With his master it was just the opposite, whose imagination immediately conjured up the whole scene vividly as one of the adventures of his books.

He took it into his head that the litter was a bier on which was borne some sorely wounded or slain knight, to avenge whom was a task reserved for him alone. Without further reasoning he laid his lance in rest, fixed himself firmly in his saddle, and with gallant spirit and bearing took up his position in the middle of the road where the white-robed riders must of necessity pass; and as soon as he saw them near at hand he raised his voice and said:

"Halt, knights, or whoever you may be, and render me account of who you are, where you come from, where you go, and what it is you carry upon that bier; for, to judge by appearances, either you have done some wrong or some wrong has been done to you, and it is fitting and necessary that I know — either so that I may chastise you for the evil you have done, or else avenge you for the injury that has been done to you."
"We are in haste," answered one of the white-robed men, "and the inn is far off, and we cannot stop to give you such an account as you demand;" and spurring his mule he moved on.

Don Quixote was mightily provoked by this answer, and seizing the mule by the bridle he said, "Halt, and be more mannerly, and render an account of what I have asked of you; or else take my defiance to combat, all of you."

The mule was shy, and was so frightened at having her bridle seized that she reared up and flung her rider over her haunches to the ground. An attendant who was on foot, seeing the white-robed man fall, began to abuse Don Quixote, who, now moved to anger, without any more ado, laying his lance in rest, charged one of the men in mourning and brought him badly wounded to the ground; and as he wheeled round upon the others, the agility with which he attacked and routed them was a sight to see — it seemed just as if wings had that instant grown on Rocinante, so lightly and proudly did he bear himself. The robed riders were all timid folk and unarmed, so they speedily made their escape from the fray and set off at a run across the plain with their lighted torches, looking exactly like masquers running on some gala or festival night. The mourners, too, enveloped and swathed in their skirts and gowns, were unable to bestir themselves; and so, in entire safety to himself, Don Quixote belaboured them all and drove them off against their will, for they all thought it was no man but a devil from hell come to carry away the dead body they had in the litter.
Sancho beheld all this in astonishment at the intrepidity of his lord, and said to himself, "Clearly this master of mine is as bold and valiant as he says he is."

A burning torch lay on the ground near the first man whom the mule had thrown, by the light of which Don Quixote noticed him, and coming up to him he presented the point of his lance to the man's face, calling on him to yield himself prisoner, or else he would kill him. To this the prostrate man replied, "I am prisoner enough as it is; I cannot stir, for one of my legs is broken. I beg you, if you be a Christian gentleman, do not kill me, for that would be grave sacrilege — I am a licentiate and I hold first orders."
"Then what the devil brought you here, being a churchman?" said Don Quixote.
"What, señor?" said the other. "My bad luck."
"Then still worse awaits you," said Don Quixote, "if you do not answer all I asked you at first."

"You shall be soon satisfied," said the licentiate. "You must know, then, that though just now I said I was a licentiate, I am only a bachelor, and my name is Alonzo Lopez; I am a native of Alcobendas; I come from the city of Baeza with eleven others, all priests — the same who fled with the torches — and we are going to the city of Segovia accompanying a dead body in that litter, the body of a gentleman who died in Baeza, where he was interred. As I said, we are now taking his bones to their burial place, which is in Segovia, where he was born."
"And who killed him?" asked Don Quixote.
"God, by means of a malignant fever that took him," answered the bachelor.

"In that case," said Don Quixote, "the Lord has relieved me of the task of avenging his death, had any other slain him; but, he who slew him having slain him, there is nothing for it but to be silent and shrug one's shoulders; I should do the same were he to slay me myself. And I would have your reverence know that I am a knight of La Mancha, Don Quixote by name, and it is my business and calling to roam the world righting wrongs and redressing injuries."

"I do not know how that about righting wrongs can be," said the bachelor, "for from straight you have made me crooked, leaving me with a broken leg that will never see itself straight again all the days of its life; and the injury you have redressed in my case has been to leave me injured in such a way that I shall remain injured forever; and the height of misfortune it was to fall in with you who go in search of adventures."

"Things do not all happen in the same way," answered Don Quixote. "It all came, Sir Bachelor Alonzo Lopez, of your going, as you did, by night, dressed in those surplices, with lighted torches, praying, covered in mourning, so that naturally you looked like something evil and of the other world; and so I could not avoid doing my duty in attacking you, and I should have attacked you even had I known for certain that you were the very devils of hell, for such I certainly believed and took you to be."

"As my fate has so willed it," said the bachelor, "I beg you, sir knight-errant, whose errand has turned out so badly for me, to help me to get from under this mule, which has caught one of my legs between the stirrup and the saddle."
"I would have talked on till tomorrow," said Don Quixote; "how long were you going to wait before telling me of your distress?"

He at once called to Sancho, who, however, had no mind to come, as he was just then engaged in unloading a pack-mule heavily laden with provisions which these worthy gentlemen had brought with them. Sancho made a bag of his coat, and, gathering as much as he could and the bag would hold, he loaded his beast, and then hastened to obey his master's call, helping him to remove the bachelor from under the mule. Then putting him on her back, he gave him the torch, and Don Quixote told him to follow the track of his companions, and to beg pardon of them on his behalf for the wrong he could not help doing them.

And Sancho said, "If by chance these gentlemen should want to know who was the hero that served them so, your worship may tell them that he is the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, otherwise called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance."
The bachelor then took his departure.
I forgot to mention that before he did so he said to Don Quixote, "Remember that you stand excommunicated for having laid violent hands on a holy thing, _juxta illud, si quis, suadente diabolo_."

"I do not understand that Latin," answered Don Quixote, "but I know well I did not lay hands — only this pike. Besides, I did not think I was committing an assault on priests or things of the Church, which, as the Catholic and faithful Christian I am, I respect and revere — but on phantoms and spectres of the other world. But even so, I remember how it fared with Cid Ruy Diaz when he broke the chair of the ambassador of that king before His Holiness the Pope, who excommunicated him for it; and yet the good Roderick of Vivar bore himself that day like a very noble and valiant knight."

On hearing this the bachelor took his departure, as has been said, without making any reply; and Don Quixote asked Sancho what had induced him to call him the "Knight of the Rueful Countenance" just then more than at any other time.

"I'll tell you," answered Sancho; "it was because I've been looking at you for some time by the light of the torch held by that unfortunate, and truly your worship has lately got the most ill-favoured countenance I ever saw. It must be either from the fatigue of this combat, or else from the loss of teeth and grinders."

"It is not that," replied Don Quixote, "but because the sage whose duty it will be to write the history of my achievements must have thought it proper that I should take some distinctive name, as all the knights of old did — one being 'He of the Burning Sword,' another 'He of the Unicorn,' this one 'He of the Damsels,' that one 'He of the Phoenix,' another 'The Knight of the Griffin,' and another 'He of the Death,' and by these names and designations they were known all the world over. And so I say that the sage I have spoken of must have put it into your mouth and mind just now to call me 'The Knight of the Rueful Countenance,' as I intend to call myself from this day forward. And so that the said name may fit me better, I mean, when the opportunity offers, to have a very rueful countenance painted on my shield."

"There is no need, señor, to waste time or money on having that countenance made," said Sancho; "all that need be done is for your worship to show your own, face to face, to those who look at you, and without anything more — image or shield — they will call you 'Him of the Rueful Countenance,' and believe me, I am telling you the truth. For I assure you, señor (and in good part be it said), hunger and the loss of your grinders have given you such an ill-favoured face that, as I say, the rueful picture may very well be spared."
Don Quixote laughed at Sancho's pleasantry; nevertheless he resolved to call himself by that name, and have his shield or buckler painted as he had devised.
Don Quixote would have looked to see whether the body in the litter was bones or not, but Sancho would not have it, saying:

"Señor, you have brought this perilous adventure to a safer end for yourself than any of those I have seen. These people, though beaten and routed, may think that it was only a single man who beat them, and feeling sore and ashamed of it, may take heart and come in search of us and give us trouble enough. The ass is in proper trim, the mountains are near at hand, hunger presses, we have nothing more to do but make good our retreat; and as the saying is, the dead to the grave and the living to the loaf."

And driving his ass before him he begged his master to follow, who, feeling that Sancho was right, did so without replying. After proceeding some little distance between two hills they found themselves in a wide, retired valley, where they dismounted; and Sancho unloaded his beast, and, stretched on the green grass with hunger for sauce, they breakfasted, dined, lunched, and supped all at once, satisfying their appetites with more than one store of cold meat that the dead man's clerical gentlemen (who seldom put themselves on short allowance) had brought with them on their pack-mule. But another piece of bad luck befell them, which Sancho held to be the worst of all: they had no wine to drink, nor even water to moisten their lips; and as thirst tormented them, Sancho, observing that the meadow where they were was full of green and tender grass, said what will be told in the following chapter.

title: Part 1, Chapter 20
paragraphs: About the unprecedented and unheard-of adventure that the brave Don Quixote of La Mancha accomplished with less danger than any famous knight in the world ever faced in any exploit

“Señor, this grass can only mean one thing: there has to be a spring or a stream close by that keeps it moist. So we would do well to move a little farther on and find some place where we can quench this terrible thirst that is tormenting us — which, without a doubt, is harder to bear than hunger.”

The advice seemed sound to Don Quixote, and so — he leading Rocinante by the bridle, and Sancho leading the donkey by the halter after packing the leftovers from supper onto its back — they moved across the meadow by feel, since the darkness of the night made it impossible to see anything. But they had not gone two hundred paces when a loud noise of water reached their ears, as if it were crashing down from high rocks. The sound cheered them enormously; but when they stopped to listen and work out which direction it was coming from, they heard, at the worst possible moment, another noise that spoiled the pleasure the sound of the water had given them — especially for Sancho, who was timid and easily frightened by nature. What they heard, I say, were blows falling with a measured rhythm, along with a certain rattling of iron and chains which, combined with the furious roar of the water, would have struck terror into any heart except Don Quixote’s. The night, as I have said, was dark, and they happened to have wandered in among some tall trees whose leaves, stirred by a gentle breeze, made a low, menacing rustle; so that what with the solitude, the location, the darkness, the noise of the water, and the whispering of the leaves, everything filled them with awe and dread — all the more because they noticed that the blows never stopped, the wind never died down, and morning never seemed to come; and on top of all that, they had no idea where they were.

But Don Quixote, sustained by his fearless heart, leaped onto Rocinante, braced his shield on his arm, lowered his pike into position, and said, “Friend Sancho, you should know that by Heaven’s will I was born into this iron age of ours to revive in it the age of gold — the golden age, as people call it. I am the man for whom dangers, mighty achievements, and brave deeds have been reserved. I am, I say again, the one who is destined to revive the Knights of the Round Table, the Twelve of France, and the Nine Worthies; the one who will consign to oblivion the Platirs, the Tablantes, the Olivantes and Tirantes, the Phœbuses and Belianises, together with the whole crowd of famous knights-errant of times past, by performing, in this age I live in, such exploits, wonders, and feats of arms that they will eclipse the brightest deeds those knights ever did. Notice well, faithful and loyal squire, the gloom of this night, its strange silence, the dull, confused murmuring of these trees, the terrifying sound of that water we came looking for, which seems to be hurling and dashing itself down from the high mountains of the Moon, and that relentless hammering that wounds and stings our ears. All these things together — and each one on its own — are enough to plant fear, dread, and panic in the chest of Mars himself, let alone in someone not accustomed to hazards and adventures of this kind. Well then, everything I have just described to you is nothing but a spur and a stimulant to my spirit, making my heart all but burst in my chest with eagerness to take on this adventure, however difficult it promises to be. So tighten Rocinante’s girths a little, and God be with you. Wait for me here three days and no longer; if I have not come back by then, you may return to our village, and from there — as a favor and a service to me — you will go to El Toboso, where you will tell my incomparable lady Dulcinea that her captive knight died attempting deeds that might make him worthy of being called hers.”
When Sancho heard his master’s words, he began to weep in the most pitiful way, saying:

“Señor, I do not understand why your worship wants to attempt such a terrifying adventure. It is night now, no one can see us here; we can easily turn around and get ourselves out of danger, even if it means not drinking for the next three days. And since there is no one to see us, there is no one to call us cowards either. Besides, I have heard the priest of our village — your worship knows him well — preach many times that whoever goes looking for danger dies in it. So it is not right to tempt God by attempting something so enormous that the only way out of it is by a miracle; and Heaven has already performed enough miracles for your worship, saving you from being tossed in a blanket the way I was, and bringing you out victorious, safe, and sound from all those enemies who were escorting the dead man. And if none of this moves or softens that hard heart of yours, then let this thought move it: the moment you leave this spot, I will be handing my soul over, out of sheer terror, to anyone willing to take it. I left my home and my wife and children to come and serve your worship, believing I would be better off for it, not worse; but just as greed bursts the bag, it has torn my hopes apart, because right when they were at their highest — about getting that miserable, unlucky island your worship has promised me so many times — I see that instead of it, and in place of it, you mean to abandon me now in a spot so far from any human soul. For God’s sake, master, do not treat me so unjustly; and if your worship absolutely will not give up attempting this feat, at least put it off until morning, because by what the lore I learned as a shepherd tells me, it cannot be three hours till dawn now — the mouth of the Horn is overhead, and it marks midnight in the line of the left arm.”

“How can you see, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “where that line falls, or where this mouth or this back-of-the-head you are talking about is, when the night is so dark that there is not a single star visible in the whole sky?”
“That is true,” said Sancho, “but fear has sharp eyes and can see things underground, let alone up in the sky. Besides, there is good reason to think it is not far off daylight now.”

“Let it be far off or not,” replied Don Quixote, “it will never be said of me, now or at any other time, that tears or pleading turned me away from doing what knightly practice required. So I ask you, Sancho, to keep quiet; for God, who has put it into my heart to undertake this unprecedented and terrifying adventure, will take care to watch over my safety and to comfort your sorrow. What you have to do is tighten Rocinante’s girths well and wait here, because I will be back shortly — alive or dead.”

Sancho, seeing that this was his master’s final decision and how little his tears, advice, and pleading had achieved, decided to fall back on his own ingenuity and force him, if he could, to wait until daylight. So, while tightening the horse’s girths, quietly and without being noticed, he used his donkey’s halter to tie both of Rocinante’s legs together, so that when Don Quixote tried to ride off he could not, since the horse could only move in hops. Seeing that his trick had worked, Sancho Panza said:

“There, señor! Heaven, moved by my tears and prayers, has arranged things so that Rocinante cannot move; and if you insist on being stubborn, spurring him and striking him, you will only anger fortune and be kicking, as they say, against the pricks.”

At this Don Quixote grew desperate, but the harder he dug his heels into the horse, the less it budged; and since he had no suspicion that the legs were tied, he thought it best to resign himself and wait either for daybreak or until Rocinante could move, firmly convinced that all this came from something other than Sancho’s cleverness. So he said to him, “Since this is how it is, Sancho, and Rocinante cannot move, I am content to wait until dawn smiles on us, even if I weep at how long it takes to come.”

“There is no need to weep,” answered Sancho, “because I will entertain your worship by telling stories from now until daylight — unless you would rather dismount and lie down to sleep a little on the green grass, the way knights-errant do, so you will be fresher when day comes and the moment arrives to attempt this extraordinary adventure you are looking forward to.”

“What are you talking about — dismounting, sleeping?” said Don Quixote. “Do you take me for one of those knights who rest in the face of danger? Sleep yourself, since you were born to sleep, or do whatever you like; I will act in the way that best fits my character.”

“Don’t be angry, master,” replied Sancho, “I didn’t mean it that way.” And coming up close to him, he put one hand on the pommel of the saddle and the other on the back of it, so that he stood hugging his master’s left thigh, not daring to move a finger’s width away from him — that was how frightened he was of the blows, which still went on sounding in a steady rhythm. Don Quixote told him to tell some story to pass the time, as he had offered, and Sancho replied that he would, if his terror at what he was hearing would let him. “Still,” he said, “I will do my best to tell a story which, if I manage to get through it and nobody interrupts the telling, is the best of stories. Pay attention, your worship, because here I begin. What was, was; and may the good that comes be for everyone, and the evil for the one who goes looking for it. Your worship should note that the opening the old folk used for their tales was not just whatever each person fancied; it was a maxim of Cato Zonzorino the Roman, the one that says ‘the evil for him that goes to look for it,’ and it fits this moment like a ring fits a finger — meaning your worship should stay put and not go looking for evil anywhere, and that we should head back by some other road, since nobody is forcing us to stay on this one where so many terrors are frightening us out of our wits.”
“Go on with your story, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “and leave the choice of our road to me.”

“So I say,” Sancho continued, “that in a village in Estremadura there was a goat-shepherd — that is, a man who tended goats — and this shepherd or goatherd, as my story goes, was called Lope Ruiz, and this Lope Ruiz was in love with a shepherdess called Torralva, and this shepherdess called Torralva was the daughter of a rich stock-farmer, and this rich stock-farmer—”

“If that is the way you are going to tell your tale, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “repeating everything you say twice over, you will not be finished in two days. Tell it straight through, like a sensible man, or else say nothing at all.”

“In my part of the country, tales are always told exactly the way I am telling this one,” answered Sancho, “and I cannot tell it any other way; nor is it fair of your worship to ask me to invent new customs.”
“Tell it however you like,” replied Don Quixote; “and since fate has decided that I have no choice but to listen to you, go on.”

“And so, lord of my soul,” Sancho went on, as I have said, this shepherd was in love with Torralva the shepherdess, who was a sturdy, headstrong girl with something slightly mannish about her, since she had the beginnings of a moustache; I can almost see her now.”
“So you knew her, then?” said Don Quixote.

“I did not know her,” said Sancho, “but the man who told me the story said it was so true and so reliable that whenever I told it to anyone else, I could safely declare and swear that I had seen it all myself. And so, as time went on, the devil — who never sleeps and stirs up trouble everywhere — arranged things so that the love the shepherd felt for the shepherdess turned into hatred and ill-will; and the cause, according to wagging tongues, was a touch of jealousy she gave him that crossed the line and strayed into forbidden territory. And from then on the shepherd hated her so much that, to get away from her, he decided to leave the district and go somewhere he would never lay eyes on her again. Torralva, the moment she found herself rejected by Lope, instantly fell in love with him, even though she had never loved him before.”
“That is the natural way of women,” said Don Quixote, “to scorn the man who loves them and love the man who hates them. Go on, Sancho.”

“It happened,” said Sancho, “that the shepherd carried out his plan, and driving his goats ahead of him, he set off across the plains of Estremadura to cross over into the Kingdom of Portugal. Torralva, who found out about it, went after him; she followed him on foot, barefoot, at a distance, with a pilgrim’s staff in her hand and a bag around her neck, in which she carried, so they say, a piece of mirror and a fragment of a comb and some little pot or other of paint for her face. But whatever she carried — I am not going to bother proving it now — all I will say is that the shepherd, the story goes, arrived with his flock at the crossing of the river Guadiana, which at that season was swollen and nearly overflowing its banks; and at the spot he came to, there was no ferry, no boat, and no one to carry him or his flock to the other side, which upset him greatly, because he could see Torralva getting closer, and he knew she would pester him no end with her tears and pleading. He kept looking around, though, so carefully that he spotted a fisherman who had beside him a boat so small that it could hold only one person and one goat; but even so, he spoke to the man and arranged for him to carry himself and his three hundred goats across. The fisherman got into the boat and carried one goat over; he came back and carried another over; he came back again, and again brought another over — and your worship had better keep count of the goats the fisherman is ferrying across, because if even one slips your memory, the story ends right there, and it will be impossible to tell another word of it. To go on, then, I should tell you that the landing place on the other side was muddy and slippery, and the fisherman lost a great deal of time going back and forth; even so, he came back for another goat, and another, and another.”
“Just take it as given that he got them all across,” said Don Quixote, “and stop going back and forth like this, or you will not finish ferrying them over in a year.”
“How many have crossed so far?” said Sancho.
“How the devil should I know?” replied Don Quixote.
“There you have it,” said Sancho, “exactly what I told you — that you had to keep a careful count. Well then, by God, the story is over, because there is no going any further.”
“How can that be?” said Don Quixote. “Is it really so essential to the story to know the exact number of goats that have crossed, that if the count is off by one, you cannot go on with it?”

“No, señor, not in the least,” replied Sancho; “because the moment I asked your worship to tell me how many goats had crossed, and you answered that you did not know, at that very instant everything I still had to tell vanished from my memory — and believe me, there was real substance in it, and entertainment too.”
“So that is it, then,” said Don Quixote — “the story has come to an end?”
“As dead as my mother is,” said Sancho.

“To tell the truth,” said Don Quixote, “you have told one of the strangest stories, tales, or histories that anyone in the world could have dreamed up, and such a way of telling it and ending it has never been seen and never will be in a lifetime — though I expected nothing less from your fine intelligence. But I am not surprised; perhaps that endless pounding has scrambled your wits.”
“That may all be so,” replied Sancho, “but as far as my story goes, all I know is that it ends right at the point where the mistake in counting the goats’ crossings begins.”

“Let it end wherever it likes, fine by me,” said Don Quixote, “and let us see whether Rocinante can move.” He spurred him again, and again Rocinante gave a few hops and stayed exactly where he was — that was how well he had been tied.

Just then — whether it was the chill of the morning that was now approaching, or something laxative he had eaten at supper, or simply nature taking its course (which is most likely) — Sancho felt the urge to do what no one else could do for him. But the fear that had seeped into his heart was so great that he did not dare move away from his master by so much as the breadth of a fingernail; yet not doing what he needed to do was equally impossible. So what he did, for the sake of peace, was to take his right hand off the back of the saddle and use it, quietly and gently, to loosen the slip-knot that was the only thing holding his breeches up, so that the moment it came undone they dropped around his ankles like shackles. Then he hitched up his shirt as best he could and bared a backside that was by no means small. Once that was done — and he imagined it was all he needed to do to escape this terrible bind and predicament — an even greater difficulty faced him: it seemed to him impossible to relieve himself without making some noise. So he clenched his teeth and hunched his shoulders together, holding his breath as hard as he could. But despite all these precautions, in the end he was unlucky enough to make a little noise — quite different from the one that was causing him so much fear.
Don Quixote heard it and said, “What noise is that, Sancho?”

“I don’t know, señor,” he said; “it must be something new — adventures and misadventures never start with trifles.” Then he tried his luck once more, and this time so successfully that, without any further noise or commotion, he found himself free of the burden that had caused him so much discomfort. But since Don Quixote’s sense of smell was as sharp as his hearing, and Sancho was pressed so tightly against him that the fumes rose almost in a straight line, some of them inevitably reached his nose; and the moment they did, he came to its rescue by pinching it between two fingers and saying, in a rather nasal tone, “Sancho, it strikes me that you are in great fear.”
“I am,” answered Sancho; “but how does your worship notice it now more than ever?”
“Because right now you smell stronger than ever — and not of ambergris,” answered Don Quixote.
“That may well be,” said Sancho, “but it is not my fault — it is your worship’s, for dragging me around at ungodly hours and at such an unnatural pace.”

“Then move back three or four paces, my friend,” said Don Quixote, keeping his fingers pinched to his nose the whole time; “and from now on, pay more attention to your person and to what you owe to mine. It is my excessive familiarity with you that has bred this contempt.”
“I’ll bet,” replied Sancho, “that your worship thinks I have done something with my person that I should not have.”
“It only makes it worse to stir it, friend Sancho,” returned Don Quixote.

With this conversation and others like it, master and servant passed the night; and when Sancho saw that dawn was coming on fast, he very cautiously untied Rocinante and tied up his breeches. As soon as Rocinante found himself free — though by nature he was anything but spirited — he seemed to come alive and began pawing the ground; as for prancing, begging his pardon, he did not know the meaning of the word. Don Quixote, seeing that Rocinante could now move, took it as a good omen and a signal that he should attempt the fearsome adventure. By now day had fully broken and everything stood out clearly, and Don Quixote saw that he was among some tall trees — chestnuts — that cast a very deep shade. He noticed too that the pounding had not stopped, though he could not see what was causing it; so without any further delay he gave Rocinante the spur, and taking leave of Sancho once more, he told him to wait there three days at most, as he had said before, and that if he had not returned by then, Sancho could be certain it had been God’s will for him to end his days in that perilous adventure. He repeated once again the message and the errand Sancho was to carry on his behalf to his lady Dulcinea, and he told him not to worry about payment for his services, because before leaving home he had made his will, in which Sancho would find himself fully compensated in the matter of wages, in proportion to the time he had served; but if God brought him out of that danger safe, sound, and unharmed, then Sancho could consider the promised island more than certain. Sancho began to weep all over again at hearing his good master’s moving words once more, and he resolved to stay with him until the very last act and end of the business. From these tears and this honorable resolution of Sancho Panza’s, the author of this history concludes that he must have been wellborn and at the very least an old Christian. The feeling he showed touched his master somewhat — but not enough to make him display any weakness; on the contrary, hiding what he felt as best he could, he began riding toward the place the sound of the water and the pounding seemed to be coming from.

Sancho followed him on foot, leading his donkey by the halter as he always did — that constant companion of his in good fortune and bad — and after they had gone some distance through the shady chestnut trees, they came out onto a small meadow at the foot of some high rocks, over which a great torrent of water hurled itself down. At the foot of the rocks stood some crudely built houses that looked more like ruins than houses, and they realized that the din and clatter of blows, which still went on without a pause, was coming from among them. Rocinante shied at the noise of the water and the blows, but Don Quixote calmed him and advanced step by step toward the houses, commending himself with all his heart to his lady and begging her to support him in that fearsome pass and enterprise — and along the way commending himself to God as well, asking not to be forgotten. Sancho, who never left his side, stretched his neck out as far as it would go and peered between Rocinante’s legs to see if he could finally make out what it was that had caused him such fear and dread. They went perhaps a hundred paces farther, and on turning a corner, the true cause — beyond any possibility of mistake — of that dreadful-sounding and, to them, terrifying noise that had kept them in such fear and confusion all night long stood revealed, plain and obvious. And it was (if you, reader, are not too disgusted and disappointed) six fulling hammers, whose alternating strokes made all the racket.

When Don Quixote saw what it was, he went mute and rigid from head to foot. Sancho glanced at him and saw him with his head sunk on his chest in obvious mortification; and Don Quixote glanced at Sancho and saw his cheeks puffed out and his mouth full of laughter, clearly about to explode with it; and despite his irritation, Don Quixote could not help laughing himself at the sight of him. And once Sancho saw that his master had started, he let loose so violently that he had to hold his sides with both hands to keep himself from bursting. Four times he calmed down, and four times the laughter broke out again with the same force as before — at which Don Quixote grew furious, above all when he heard him say, mockingly, “You must know, friend Sancho, that by Heaven’s will I was born in this our iron age to revive in it the golden age, or age of gold; I am he for whom are reserved dangers, mighty achievements, brave deeds” — and so he went on, repeating the very words Don Quixote had spoken when they first heard the terrifying blows.

Don Quixote, seeing that Sancho was making fun of him, was so humiliated and angry that he raised his pike and landed two blows on him — blows so hard that if they had caught him on the head instead of on the shoulders, there would have been no wages left to pay, except perhaps to his heirs. Sancho, finding that his joke was earning him a painfully serious return, and afraid his master might take it even further, said to him very humbly, “Calm down, sir — by God, I am only joking.”
