“Well, you may be joking, but I am not,” replied Don Quixote. “Come here, my merry gentleman: do you think that if these had been some dangerous adventure instead of fulling hammers, I would not have shown the courage needed to take it on and see it through? Am I, being the gentleman I am, somehow obliged to recognize sounds and tell them apart, and know whether they come from fulling mills or not — when it may well be, as is in fact the case, that I have never in my life laid eyes on one, unlike you, lowborn peasant that you are, who were born and raised among them? But turn these six hammers into six giants and send them against me, one by one or all together, and if I do not knock every one of them flat on his back, then mock me as much as you please.”

“No more of that, señor,” returned Sancho; “I admit I carried the joke a bit too far. But tell me, your worship, now that we have made peace — and may God bring you out of every adventure that comes your way as safe and sound as he has brought you out of this one — was it not something worth laughing at, and does it not make a good story, the great fright we were in? At least the fright I was in; because as for your worship, I see now that you do not know or understand what fear or dismay even is.”
“I do not deny,” said Don Quixote, “that what happened to us is worth laughing at; but it is not worth telling as a story, because not everyone is sharp enough to see the right point of a thing.”

“At any rate,” said Sancho, “your worship certainly knew how to hit the right point with your pike — aiming at my head and landing on my shoulders, thanks be to God and to my own quickness in dodging. But never mind; it will all come out in the wash. I have heard it said that ‘the one who loves you well is the one who makes you cry’; and besides, great lords, after giving a servant a harsh word, usually give him a pair of breeches — though I do not know what they give after a beating, unless it is that knights-errant, after beatings, hand out islands, or kingdoms on the mainland.”

“The dice may fall,” said Don Quixote, “in such a way that everything you say comes true. Forgive what is past, since you are sharp enough to know that our first impulses are not within our control; and from now on, bear one thing in mind: that you curb and restrain your chatter in my company. In all the books of chivalry I have read — and they are countless — I have never come across a squire who talked as much to his lord as you do to yours. And honestly, I consider it a serious fault, both yours and mine: yours, in that you show me so little respect; mine, in that I do not make myself more respected. There was Gandalin, the squire of Amadis of Gaul, who became Count of the Insula Firme; and we read of him that he always addressed his lord with his cap in his hand, his head bowed and his body bent double, more turquesco, as the Turks do. And then what shall we say of Gasabal, the squire of Galaor, who was so silent that, to convey to us the greatness of his marvelous taciturnity, his name is mentioned only once in the whole of that history, long and truthful as it is? From everything I have said, Sancho, you should gather that there has to be a difference between master and servant, between lord and lackey, between knight and squire; so from this day forward, in our dealings with each other, we must show more respect and take fewer liberties, because however you manage to provoke me, it will be the pitcher that pays for it. The favors and rewards I have promised you will arrive in due time; and if they do not, your wages, at least, will not be lost, as I have already told you.”

“Everything your worship says is all very well,” said Sancho, “but I would like to know — just in case the time of favors never comes and it becomes necessary to fall back on wages — how much did a knight-errant’s squire earn in those days? And did they agree on terms by the month, or by the day, like bricklayers?”

“I do not believe,” replied Don Quixote, “that squires of that kind were ever paid wages; they depended on favor. And if I have now provided for yours in the sealed will I left at home, it was with an eye to whatever might happen; for I still do not know how chivalry will fare in these wretched times of ours, and I would not want my soul to suffer in the next world over trifles. Because I would have you know, Sancho, that in this world there is no calling more dangerous than that of adventurers.”

“That is true enough,” said Sancho, “seeing that the mere noise of the hammers of a fulling mill can disturb and unsettle the heart of as brave an errant adventurer as your worship. But you can be sure that from now on I will not open my lips to make light of anything of your worship’s — only to honor you as my master and natural lord.”
“If you do that,” replied Don Quixote, “you will live long on the face of the earth; for after our parents, our masters deserve to be respected as though they were our parents themselves.”

title: Part 1, Chapter 21
paragraphs: Which treats of the great adventure and rich prize of Mambrino's helmet, and other things that happened to our invincible knight

It was beginning to rain a little, and Sancho wanted to take shelter in the fulling mills, but Don Quixote had developed such a loathing for them after the recent joke that he refused to enter on any account. So they turned aside to the right and came upon another road, different from the one they had taken the night before. Shortly afterwards Don Quixote spotted a man on horseback wearing on his head something that shone like gold, and the moment he saw him he turned to Sancho and said:

"I don't think there's a proverb that isn't true, Sancho, since they're all maxims drawn from experience itself, the mother of all the sciences — especially the one that says, 'Where one door shuts, another opens.' I mention this because, if last night fortune slammed the door on the adventure we were after by cheating us with the fulling mills, it's now throwing open another door wide on a better and more certain adventure. If I fail to walk through it, the fault will be mine alone, and I won't be able to blame it on my ignorance of fulling mills or the darkness of the night. I say this because, unless I'm much mistaken, the man approaching us is wearing on his head the helmet of Mambrino — the very helmet I swore that oath about, as you'll remember."
"Watch what you say, your worship, and even more what you do," said Sancho, "because I don't want any more fulling mills around to finish the job of pounding our wits out of us."
"The devil take you, man," said Don Quixote. "What does a helmet have to do with fulling mills?"
"I don't know," Sancho replied, "but honestly, if I were free to speak the way I used to, I could maybe give you reasons that would show your worship you're mistaken in what you're saying."

"How can I be mistaken in what I say, you unbelieving traitor?" Don Quixote shot back. "Tell me, don't you see that knight coming towards us on a dappled grey steed, with a helmet of gold on his head?"
"All I can see and make out," answered Sancho, "is a man on a grey ass like mine, with something shiny on his head."

"Well, that is the helmet of Mambrino," said Don Quixote. "Stand off to one side and leave me alone with him. You'll see how, without wasting a word, to save time, I bring this adventure to a finish and take possession of the helmet I've longed for so much."
"I'll make sure to stand aside," said Sancho, "but God grant — I say it again — that it turn out to be marjoram and not fulling mills."
"I told you, brother, on no account to mention those fulling mills to me again," said Don Quixote, "or I swear — and I'll say no more — I'll full the soul out of you."
Sancho held his tongue, afraid his master might actually carry out the vow he'd hurled at him like a bowling ball.

Here's what was really going on with that helmet, steed, and knight Don Quixote was seeing. In that area there were two villages, one of them so small it had neither pharmacy nor barber, while the other nearby had both. So the barber of the larger one served the smaller, and in the smaller village there was a sick man who needed bleeding and another man who wanted a shave. The barber was on his way to do both, carrying a brass basin with him; but as luck would have it, on the way it began to rain, and to keep his hat (probably a new one) from getting ruined, he put the basin on his head. The basin, being clean, glittered at half a league's distance. He rode on a grey ass, just as Sancho said, and this was what made Don Quixote see it as a dappled grey steed, a knight, and a golden helmet — because he made everything he saw fit in with his crazy chivalry and ill-errant notions. So when he saw the poor knight draw near, without bothering with any parley, at Rocinante's top speed he bore down on him with his pike lowered, fully determined to run him clean through; and as he reached him, without checking the fury of his charge, he shouted:
"Defend yourself, you wretched creature, or surrender of your own accord what is so reasonably my due."

The barber, who had no warning or even any suspicion this apparition was bearing down on him, had no other way of saving himself from the lance-stroke than to let himself drop off his ass; and the moment he hit the ground he sprang up more nimbly than a deer and sped away across the plain faster than the wind.

He left the basin on the ground, and Don Quixote was satisfied with that, remarking that the pagan had shown good sense and imitated the beaver, which, when pressed by hunters, bites off with its teeth the very thing its instinct tells it they are pursuing.
He told Sancho to pick up the helmet, and Sancho, taking it in his hands, said:

"By God, the basin's a good one, and worth a real of eight if it's worth a maravedí," and handed it to his master, who immediately put it on his head, turning it this way and that in search of the visor; and not finding one, he said, "Clearly the pagan to whose measure this famous head-piece was first forged must have had an enormous head; but the worst of it is, half of it is missing."
When Sancho heard him call the basin a head-piece, he couldn't hold back his laughter; but remembering his master's wrath, he checked himself in the middle of it.
"What are you laughing at, Sancho?" said Don Quixote.
"I'm laughing," he said, "at the thought of the huge head the pagan must have had who owned this helmet, because it looks exactly like an ordinary barber's basin."

"Do you know what I suspect, Sancho?" said Don Quixote. "That this marvellous piece, this enchanted helmet, must by some strange accident have come into the hands of someone who couldn't recognise or appreciate its value, and who, not knowing what he was doing and seeing it was of the purest gold, melted down one half for its worth, and out of the other made this thing that, as you say, looks like a barber's basin. Be that as it may, it makes no difference to me — I recognise it — and I'll have it set right at the first village where there's a blacksmith, in such style that not even the helmet the god of smithies forged for the god of battle will surpass it or even come close. In the meantime I'll wear it as well as I can, because something is better than nothing, and it'll certainly be enough to protect me from any chance blow of a stone."

"That is," said Sancho, "if it isn't shot with a sling like in the battle of the two armies, when they signed the cross on your worship's grinders and smashed the flask with that blessed brew that made me vomit up my guts."
"It doesn't grieve me much to have lost it," said Don Quixote, "because you know, Sancho, that I have the recipe in my memory."

"So do I," answered Sancho, "but if I ever make it, or try it again as long as I live, may this be my last hour. Besides, I don't intend to put myself anywhere near needing it, for I mean, with all five of my senses, to keep myself from getting wounded or from wounding anyone. As to being blanket-tossed again, I'll say nothing, since it's hard to prevent mishaps of that sort, and if they come there's nothing for it but to squeeze our shoulders together, hold our breath, shut our eyes, and let ourselves go wherever luck and the blanket send us."

"You're a bad Christian, Sancho," said Don Quixote on hearing this, "because once an injury's been done to you, you never forget it. But know this: it is the mark of noble and generous hearts not to attach importance to trifles. What lame leg have you got from it, what broken rib, what cracked head, that you can't forget that joke? For joke and sport it was, properly understood; and if I hadn't seen it that way, I'd have gone back and done more mischief avenging you than the Greeks did for the rape of Helen — who, if she were alive now, or if my Dulcinea had lived then, you can depend on it would not be so famous for her beauty as she is." And here he heaved a sigh and sent it aloft. Said Sancho, "Let it pass for a joke, since it can't be avenged in earnest; but I know what sort of joke and what sort of earnest it was, and I know it'll never be rubbed out of my memory any more than off my shoulders. But putting that aside, will your worship tell me what we're to do with this dappled grey steed that looks like a grey ass, which that Martino your worship overthrew has left behind? Because from the way he took to his heels and bolted, he's not likely ever to come back for it; and by my beard, the grey is a good one."

"I've never been in the habit," said Don Quixote, "of taking spoils from those I defeat, nor is it chivalry's practice to take the horses of the vanquished and leave them to walk — unless, that is, the victor has lost his own horse in the combat, in which case it's lawful to take the vanquished's mount as a thing won in lawful war. So, Sancho, leave this horse, or ass, or whatever you want to call it; when its owner sees us gone, he'll come back for it."

"God knows I'd like to take it," Sancho replied, "or at least swap it for my own, which doesn't seem as good. Truly the laws of chivalry are strict, since they can't be stretched to let one ass be swapped for another. I'd like to know if I might at least trade trappings."
"On that I'm not entirely certain," answered Don Quixote, "and the matter being doubtful, pending better information, I say you may swap them, if you have urgent need."

"So urgent," answered Sancho, "that if they were for my own person I couldn't want them more." And immediately, fortified by this permission, he carried out the _mutatio capparum_, rigging out his beast to the ninety-nines and turning it into quite a different thing. With that done, they broke their fast on the remains of the spoils plundered from the pack-mule and drank from the brook that flowed down from the fulling mills, without casting so much as a glance in their direction, so much did they loathe them for the alarm they'd caused. All anger and gloom now gone, they mounted up and, without taking any fixed road (refusing to fix on one being the proper thing for true knights-errant), set out guided by Rocinante's will, which carried along with it that of his master and, for that matter, of the ass, which always followed him wherever he led, lovingly and sociably. Eventually they came back to the high road and pursued it at random with no particular aim.

As they rode along this way, Sancho said to his master, "Señor, would your worship give me leave to speak a little? Since you laid that hard injunction of silence on me, several things have rotted in my stomach, and I have one right now on the tip of my tongue that I don't want to be spoiled."
"Speak on, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and be brief, for there's no pleasure in a long-winded speech."

"Well then, señor," Sancho replied, "I've been thinking these past few days about how little is got or gained by hunting these adventures your worship goes looking for in these wilds and crossroads, where, even when the most perilous ones are won, there's no one to see or know of them, and so they have to be left untold forever — to the loss of your worship's purpose and the credit they deserve. It seems to me it would be better (saving your worship's better judgment) if we went and served some emperor or other great prince who had a war on his hands. In his service your worship could prove the worth of your person, your great strength, and your even greater understanding, and on seeing it, the lord we served would have to reward us, each according to his merits; and there you wouldn't lack for someone to set down your achievements in writing so as to preserve their memory forever. About my own I'll say nothing, since they won't go beyond squirely limits — though I make bold to say that, if it's the practice in chivalry to write down the achievements of squires, I think mine shouldn't be left out."

"You don't speak amiss, Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "but before that point is reached we have to roam the world, as it were on probation, seeking adventures, so that by completing a few, the knight may earn a name and fame such that when he presents himself at the court of some great monarch he is already known by his deeds — and the boys, the instant they see him enter the city gate, will all follow him and surround him, shouting, 'This is the Knight of the Sun!' — or of the Serpent, or whatever title under which he achieved his great deeds. 'This,' they will say, 'is the one who defeated in single combat the gigantic Brocabruno of mighty strength; the one who delivered the great Mameluke of Persia from the long enchantment under which he'd lain for almost nine hundred years.' So they'll go from one to another, proclaiming his achievements; and presently, at the commotion of the boys and the rest, the king of that kingdom will appear at the windows of his royal palace, and as soon as he sees the knight, recognising him by his arms and the device on his shield, he'll naturally say, 'What ho! Come forth, all you knights of my court, to receive the flower of chivalry who comes here!' At which command all will issue forth, and the king himself, advancing half-way down the stairs, will embrace him closely and greet him with a kiss on the cheek, and then lead him to the queen's chamber, where the knight will find her with her daughter the princess, who will be one of the most beautiful and accomplished damsels you could find anywhere in the known world even with the most exhaustive search. The instant it comes to pass, she will fix her eyes on the knight and he his on her, and each will seem to the other something more divine than human, and, without knowing how or why, they will be caught and tangled in the inextricable toils of love, distressed in their hearts at seeing no way to make their pains and longings known by speech. From there they'll lead him, no doubt, to some richly adorned chamber of the palace, where, having removed his armour, they'll bring him a rich scarlet mantle to put on, and if he looked noble in his armour, he'll look still nobler in a doublet. When night comes he'll dine with the king, queen, and princess; and the whole time he'll never take his eyes off her, stealing glances unnoticed by those present, and she will do the same, with equal stealth, being, as I said, a damsel of great discretion. The tables being cleared, suddenly through the door of the hall there will enter a hideous little dwarf followed by a fair lady between two giants, who comes with a certain adventure devised by an ancient sage; and whoever completes it shall be reckoned the best knight in the world.

"The king will then order all those present to attempt it, and none will bring it to a finish except the stranger knight — to the great enhancement of his fame, at which the princess will be overjoyed and consider herself happy and fortunate to have set her thoughts so high. And the best of it is that this king, or prince, or whatever he is, is locked in a very bitter war with another as powerful as himself, and the stranger knight, after spending some days at his court, asks his leave to go and serve him in that war. The king will grant it very readily, and the knight will courteously kiss his hands in gratitude for the favour. That night he'll take leave of his lady the princess at the grating of the chamber where she sleeps, which looks out on a garden, and at which he has already conversed with her many times, the go-between and confidante being a damsel much trusted by the princess. He will sigh, she will swoon, the damsel will fetch water, much distressed because morning is approaching, and for her lady's honour she wouldn't want them to be discovered. At last the princess will come to herself and will offer her white hands through the grating to the knight, who will kiss them a thousand and a thousand times, bathing them with his tears. It will be arranged between them how they are to inform each other of their good or evil fortunes, and the princess will beg him to make his absence as short as possible, which he will promise to do with many oaths; once more he kisses her hands, and takes his leave in such grief that he is nearly ready to die. He goes to his chamber, flings himself on his bed, can't sleep for the sorrow of parting, rises early in the morning, goes to take leave of the king, queen, and princess, and as he takes his leave of the pair, he is told that the princess is unwell and cannot receive a visit. The knight thinks it's from grief at his departure, his heart is pierced, and he can hardly keep from showing his pain. The confidante is present, observes everything, goes to tell her mistress, who listens in tears and says that one of her greatest distresses is not knowing who this knight is, and whether he is of royal lineage or not. The damsel assures her that such courtesy, gentleness, and grace of bearing as her knight possesses could not exist in anyone but a royal and illustrious man. Her anxiety thus relieved, she strives to be of good cheer so as not to arouse her parents' suspicion, and after two days she appears in public. Meanwhile the knight has set off; he fights in the war, defeats the king's enemy, takes many cities, triumphs in many battles, returns to the court, sees his lady where he used to see her, and it is agreed that he shall ask her parents for her hand in marriage as the reward of his services. The king is unwilling to give her, as he doesn't know who he is; but nevertheless, whether carried off or by some other means, the princess becomes his bride, and her father comes to regard it as great good fortune; for it so happens that this knight is proved to be the son of a valiant king of some kingdom or other — I don't know which, since I don't expect it's on the map. The father dies, the princess inherits, and in short, the knight becomes king. And here at once comes the bestowal of rewards on his squire and on all who helped him rise to so exalted a rank. He marries his squire to one of the princess's damsels — who will no doubt be the one who was confidante in their love affair, and who is the daughter of a very great duke."
"That's what I want, no mistake about it!" said Sancho. "That's what I'm waiting for! All this, word for word, is in store for your worship under the title of the Knight of the Rueful Countenance."

"You needn't doubt it, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "because in the very same manner and by the very steps I've described, knights-errant rise — and have risen — to be kings and emperors. All we need now is to find out what king, Christian or pagan, is at war and has a beautiful daughter; but there'll be time enough to think about that, since, as I've told you, fame has to be won in other quarters before turning to court. There's another thing wanting, too: supposing we find a king who's at war and has a beautiful daughter, and that I've won incredible fame throughout the universe, I don't know how it can be made out that I'm of royal lineage, or even second cousin to an emperor; for the king won't be willing to give me his daughter in marriage unless he's first thoroughly satisfied on that point, however much my famous deeds may deserve it. So through this one deficiency I'm afraid I'll lose what my arm has fairly earned. True, I am a gentleman of known house, of estate and property, and entitled to the five hundred sueldos mulct; and it may well be that the sage who writes my history will so clear up my ancestry and pedigree that I'll find myself fifth or sixth in descent from a king. For you should know, Sancho, that there are two kinds of lineages in the world: some trace and derive their descent from kings and princes, whom time has slowly reduced until they end in a point like an upside-down pyramid; and others spring from the common herd and rise step by step until they become great lords. So the difference is that the one were what they no longer are, and the others are what they formerly were not. And I may be of such a kind that on investigation my origin will prove great and famous, which ought to satisfy the king, my father-in-law-to-be. And if it doesn't, the princess will love me so much that even if she knew perfectly well I was the son of a water-carrier, she'd take me for her lord and husband in spite of her father; and if not, then it comes to seizing her and carrying her off wherever I please; for time or death will put an end to her parents' wrath."

"This is where it comes to," said Sancho, "what some naughty people say: 'Never ask as a favour what you can take by force' — though it would fit better to say, 'A clean escape is better than good men's prayers.' I say it because if the king, your worship's father-in-law, won't condescend to give you my lady the princess, there's nothing for it, as your worship says, but to seize her and carry her off. But the trouble is that until peace is made and you come into the peaceful enjoyment of your kingdom, the poor squire is famishing as far as rewards go — unless the confidante damsel who's to be his wife comes with the princess, and with her he tides over his bad luck until Heaven orders things differently; because his master, I suppose, may as well give her to him at once for a lawful wife."
"No one can object to that," said Don Quixote.
"Well then, since that's settled," said Sancho, "there's nothing for it but to commend ourselves to God and let fortune take whatever course it will."
"God guide it according to my wishes and your needs," said Don Quixote, "and mean be he who thinks himself mean."
"In God's name let him be so," said Sancho. "I'm an old Christian, and to qualify me for a count that's enough."

"And more than enough for you," said Don Quixote, "and even if you weren't, it would make no difference, because, being king, I can easily give you nobility without your purchasing it or rendering any service; for when I make you a count, you become a gentleman at once — and they may say what they like, but by my faith they'll have to call you 'your lordship,' whether they like it or not."
"Not a doubt of it; and I'll know how to support the tittle," said Sancho.
"Title you should say, not tittle," said his master.

"So be it," answered Sancho. "I say I'll know how to behave, because once in my life I was beadle of a brotherhood, and the beadle's gown sat so well on me that everyone said I looked as if I were going to be steward of the same brotherhood. What will it be like, then, when I put a duke's robe on my back, or dress myself in gold and pearls like a count? I believe they'll come a hundred leagues just to see me."

"You'll look fine," said Don Quixote, "but you'll have to shave your beard often, since you've got it so thick and rough and tangled that if you don't shave every second day at least, they'll see what you are at the distance of a musket shot."
"What more is it," said Sancho, "than having a barber and keeping him on wages in the house? And even if necessary, I'll make him walk behind me like a nobleman's equerry."
"Why, how do you know that noblemen have equerries walking behind them?" asked Don Quixote.

"I'll tell you," answered Sancho. "Years ago I was for a month in the capital, and there I saw a very small gentleman taking the air, who they said was a very great man, and a man following him on horseback at every turn he took, as if he were his tail. I asked why this man didn't join the other instead of always walking behind him; they told me he was his equerry, and that it was the custom with nobles to have such persons behind them. Ever since then I've known it, because I've never forgotten it."

"You're right," said Don Quixote, "and in the same way you may carry your barber with you, since customs didn't all come into use together, nor were they all invented at once; and you may be the first count to have a barber follow him — and indeed, shaving one's beard is a greater trust than saddling one's horse."
"Let the barber business be my problem," said Sancho, "and your worship's be to strive to become a king and make me a count."
"So it shall be," answered Don Quixote, and raising his eyes he saw what will be told in the following chapter.

title: Part 1, Chapter 22
paragraphs: About the freedom Don Quixote conferred on several unfortunates who were being taken, against their will, where they had no wish to go

Cid Hamete Benengeli, the Arab and Manchegan author, relates in this most grave, high-sounding, minute, delightful, and original history that, after the discussion between the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha and his squire Sancho Panza recorded at the end of chapter twenty-one, Don Quixote raised his eyes and saw, coming along the road he was following, some dozen men on foot strung together by the neck like beads on a great iron chain, all with manacles on their hands. Along with them came two men on horseback and two on foot; those on horseback armed with wheel-lock muskets, those on foot with javelins and swords. As soon as Sancho saw them he said:
"That's a chain of galley slaves, on their way to the galleys by force of the king's orders."
"How by force?" asked Don Quixote. "Is it possible the king uses force against anyone?"
"I don't say that," answered Sancho, "but that these are people condemned for their crimes to serve by force in the king's galleys."
"In fact," replied Don Quixote, "however it may be, these people are being taken by force, not of their own will."
"Just so," said Sancho.
"Then if so," said Don Quixote, "here's a case for the exercise of my office — to put down force and to succour and help the wretched."
"Recall, your worship," said Sancho, "that Justice, which is the king himself, is not using force or doing wrong to such persons, but punishing them for their crimes."

By now the chain of galley slaves had come up, and Don Quixote, in very courteous language, asked those in charge of it to be so good as to tell him the reason or reasons they were conducting these people in this manner. One of the mounted guards answered that they were galley slaves belonging to his majesty, that they were on their way to the galleys, and that was all that was to be said and all he had any business knowing.

"Nevertheless," replied Don Quixote, "I'd like to know from each of them separately the reason for his misfortune." He added more in the same vein, asking so civilly that the other mounted guard said to him:

"Though we have here the register and certificate of every one of these wretches' sentences, this is no time to take them out or read them. Come and ask the men themselves; they can tell you if they choose, and they will, because these fellows take pleasure in doing and talking about rascalities."
With this permission — which Don Quixote would have taken even if they hadn't given it — he approached the chain and asked the first man what offences had brought him to such a sorry state.
The man answered that it was for being a lover.
"For that alone?" replied Don Quixote. "Why, if for being lovers they send people to the galleys, I might have been rowing in them long ago."

"The love is not the kind your worship has in mind," said the galley slave. "Mine was that I loved a washerwoman's basket of clean linen so much, and held it so close in my embrace, that if the arm of the law hadn't pulled it from me, I'd never have let it go of my own will to this day. I was caught in the act, there was no need for torture, the case was settled, they treated me to a hundred lashes on the back and three years of _gurapas_ on top of it, and that was the end of it."
"What are _gurapas_?" asked Don Quixote.
"_Gurapas_ are galleys," answered the galley slave, who was a young man of about twenty-four and said he was a native of Piedrahita.

Don Quixote asked the same question of the second, who made no reply, so downcast and melancholy was he; but the first answered for him and said, "He, sir, is going as a canary — I mean, as a musician and singer."
"What!" said Don Quixote. "For being musicians and singers, are people sent to the galleys too?"
"Yes, sir," answered the galley slave, "because there is nothing worse than singing under suffering."
"On the contrary, I've heard it said," said Don Quixote, "that he who sings scares away his woes."
"Here it's the reverse," said the galley slave, "for he who sings once weeps all his life."

"I don't understand it," said Don Quixote. But one of the guards said to him, "Sir, to sing under suffering means, with the _non sancta_ fraternity, to confess under torture. They put this sinner to the torture and he confessed his crime, which was being a _cuatrero_ — that is, a cattle thief — and on his confession they sentenced him to six years in the galleys, on top of two hundred lashes he's already had on the back. He's always dejected and downcast because the other thieves who were left behind and the ones marching here mistreat, snub, jeer at, and despise him for confessing and not having the spirit to say no; because, they say, 'no' has no more letters in it than 'yes,' and a culprit is well off when life or death depends on his own tongue and not on witnesses or evidence. To my mind, they're not far wrong."

"I think so too," answered Don Quixote. Then passing on to the third, he asked him the same question, and the man answered very readily and unconcernedly, "I'm going for five years to their ladyships the _gurapas_ for want of ten ducats."
"I'll give twenty with pleasure to get you out of that trouble," said Don Quixote.

"That," said the galley slave, "is like a man having money at sea when he's dying of hunger and has no way of buying what he wants. I say so because if at the right time I'd had those twenty ducats your worship is offering me now, I'd have greased the notary's pen and freshened up the attorney's wit with them, so that today I'd be in the middle of the plaza of the Zocodover in Toledo, and not on this road coupled like a greyhound. But God is great; patience — there, that's enough of it."

Don Quixote passed on to the fourth, a man of venerable appearance with a white beard falling below his chest, who on hearing himself asked the reason for his being there began to weep without answering a word. But the fifth acted as his tongue and said, "This worthy man is going to the galleys for four years, after having gone through the rounds in ceremony and on horseback."
"That means," said Sancho Panza, "as I take it, to have been publicly shamed."

"Just so," replied the galley slave, "and the offence for which they gave him that punishment was having been an ear-broker — no, a body-broker. In short, this gentleman is going as a pimp, and besides that for having a certain touch of the sorcerer about him."

"If that touch hadn't been thrown in," said Don Quixote, "for mere pimping he wouldn't deserve to row in the galleys but rather to command and be admiral of them, since the office of pimp is no ordinary one — it's the office of persons of discretion, very necessary in a well-ordered state, and only to be exercised by persons of good birth. In fact there ought to be an inspector and overseer of them, as in other offices, and a recognised number, as with the brokers on change; in this way many of the evils caused by this office and calling being in the hands of stupid and ignorant people would be avoided — silly women, and pages and jesters of little standing and experience, who on the most urgent occasions, and when ingenuity is needed, let the crumbs freeze on the way to their mouths and don't know which is their right hand. I'd like to go further and give reasons to show why it's advisable to choose those who are to hold so necessary an office in the state, but this isn't the right place for it. Someday I'll lay the matter out to someone able to see to it and rectify it. All I'll say now is that the additional fact of his being a sorcerer has removed the sorrow it gave me to see these white hairs and this venerable face in so painful a position on account of his being a pimp — though I'm well aware there are no sorceries in the world that can move or compel the will, as some simple folk imagine, since our will is free, and there's no herb or charm that can force it. All that certain silly women and quacks do is to drive men mad with potions and poisons, pretending they have the power to cause love; but, as I say, it's impossible to compel the will."

"It's true," said the good old man, "and indeed, sir, as far as the charge of sorcery goes I wasn't guilty; as for being a pimp, I can't deny it. But I never thought I was doing any harm by it, since my only object was that everyone should enjoy themselves and live in peace and quiet, without quarrels or troubles. But my good intentions weren't enough to save me from going where I never expect to come back from, with this weight of years on me and a urinary ailment that never gives me a moment's ease." And again he began to weep as before, and Sancho felt such compassion for him that he took out a real of four from his bosom and gave it to him in alms.
Don Quixote went on and asked another what his crime was, and the man answered with no less — rather with much more — liveliness than the last one.

"I'm here because I carried the joke too far with a couple of cousins of mine, and with a couple of other cousins who weren't mine. In short, I carried the joke so far with them all that it ended in such a complicated increase of kindred no accountant could make sense of it. It was all proved against me, I got no favour, I had no money, I was on the verge of having my neck stretched; they sentenced me to six years in the galleys, I accepted my fate, it's the punishment of my fault. I'm a young man — let my life only last, and with that everything will come right. If you, sir, have anything to help the poor, God will repay you in heaven, and we on earth will take care in our prayers to him to pray for the life and health of your worship, that they may be as long and as good as your friendly appearance deserves."
This one was dressed as a student, and one of the guards said he was a great talker and a very elegant Latin scholar.

Behind all these came a man of thirty, a very personable fellow, except that one of his eyes turned in a little towards the other when he looked at you. He was bound differently from the rest, for he had a chain on his leg so long that it was wound all round his body, and two rings on his neck, one attached to the chain, the other to what they call a "keep-friend" or "friend's foot," from which hung two irons reaching to his waist with two manacles fixed to them, in which his hands were secured by a big padlock, so that he could neither raise his hands to his mouth nor lower his head to his hands. Don Quixote asked why this man carried so many more chains than the others. The guard replied it was because he alone had committed more crimes than all the rest put together, and was so daring and such a villain that even marching him in that fashion they didn't feel sure of him but were afraid he'd escape.
"What crimes can he have committed," said Don Quixote, "if they've earned him no heavier punishment than being sent to the galleys?"

"He goes for ten years," replied the guard, "which amounts to civil death; and all that need be said is that this good fellow is the famous Gines de Pasamonte, otherwise called Ginesillo de Parapilla."

"Easy now, señor commissary," said the galley slave at this. "Let's have no fixing of names or surnames. My name is Gines, not Ginesillo, and my family name is Pasamonte, not Parapilla as you say. Let each of us mind his own business, and he'll be doing plenty."
"Speak with less impertinence, master thief of extra measure," replied the commissary, "if you don't want me to make you hold your tongue in spite of your teeth."
"It's easy to see," returned the galley slave, "that a man goes as God pleases; but someone will know one day whether I'm called Ginesillo de Parapilla or not."
"Don't they call you that, you liar?" said the guard.

"They do," returned Gines, "but I'll make them stop calling me so, or I'll be shaved where I only say behind my teeth. If you, sir, have anything to give us, give it to us at once, and God speed you, for you're becoming tiresome with all this prying into the lives of others. If you want to know about mine, let me tell you I'm Gines de Pasamonte, whose life is written by these fingers."
"He speaks the truth," said the commissary, "for he's himself written his story as grand as you please, and has left the book in the prison pawned for two hundred reals."
"And I mean to get it out of pawn," said Gines, "even if it were in for two hundred ducats."
"Is it so good?" said Don Quixote.

"So good is it," replied Gines, "that a fig for _Lazarillo de Tormes_ and all of that kind that have been written, or shall be written, compared with it. All I'll say about it is that it deals with facts, and facts so neat and amusing that no lies could match them."
"And what's the book's title?" asked Don Quixote.
"_The Life of Gines de Pasamonte_," replied its subject.
"And is it finished?" asked Don Quixote.
"How can it be finished," said the other, "when my life isn't yet finished? All that's written is from my birth down to the point when they sent me to the galleys this last time."
"Then you've been there before?" said Don Quixote.

"In the service of God and the king I've been there for four years before, and I know by this time what the biscuit and the lash are like," replied Gines. "And it's no great hardship to me to go back to them, because there I'll have time to finish my book. I still have many things left to say, and in the galleys of Spain there's more than enough leisure — though I don't need much for what I have to write, since I have it by heart."
"You seem a clever fellow," said Don Quixote.
"And an unfortunate one," replied Gines, "because misfortune always persecutes good wit."
"It persecutes rogues," said the commissary.

"I told you already to go gently, master commissary," said Pasamonte. "Their lordships yonder didn't give you that staff to mistreat us wretches here, but to conduct us and take us where his majesty orders. If not, by the life of — never mind — it may be that someday the stains made in the inn will come out in the scouring. Let everyone hold his tongue and behave well and speak better; and now let's march on, for we've had quite enough of this entertainment."

The commissary raised his staff to strike Pasamonte for his threats, but Don Quixote stepped between them and begged him not to mistreat him, since it wasn't too much to allow one who had his hands tied to have his tongue a little free. And turning to the whole chain he said:

"From all you've told me, dear brethren, I make out clearly that though they've punished you for your faults, the punishments you're about to endure don't please you much, and that you go to them very much against the grain and against your will, and that perhaps this one's lack of courage under torture, that one's lack of money, the other's lack of advocacy, and finally the perverted judgment of the judge may have caused your ruin and your failure to obtain the justice you had on your side. All of which now presents itself to my mind, urging, persuading, and even compelling me to demonstrate in your case the purpose for which Heaven sent me into the world and made me profess the order of chivalry to which I belong, and the vow I took there to give aid to those in need and under the oppression of the strong. But since I know that it's a mark of prudence not to do by foul means what may be done by fair, I'll ask these gentlemen the guards and the commissary to be so good as to release you and let you go in peace, since there'll be no lack of others to serve the king under more favourable circumstances. It seems to me a hard thing to make slaves of those whom God and nature have made free. Moreover, sirs of the guard," added Don Quixote, "these poor fellows have done nothing to you; let each answer for his own sins yonder. There is a God in Heaven who won't forget to punish the wicked or reward the good, and it isn't fitting that honest men should be the instruments of punishment to others, having no concern in the matter. This request I make gently and quietly, so that if you comply with it, I'll have reason to thank you; and if you won't do it willingly, this lance and sword together with the might of my arm shall compel you to comply with it by force."

"Nice nonsense!" said the commissary. "A fine piece of pleasantry he's come out with at last! He wants us to let the king's prisoners go, as if we had any authority to release them, or he to order us to do so! Go your way, sir, and good luck to you; straighten that basin you've got on your head, and don't go looking for three feet on a cat."

"You're the cat, the rat, and the rascal!" replied Don Quixote; and acting on the word, he fell upon him so suddenly that without giving him time to defend himself he brought him to the ground sorely wounded with a lance-thrust; and lucky it was for Don Quixote that this was the one with the musket. The other guards stood thunderstruck and amazed at this unexpected event, but recovering their presence of mind, those on horseback seized their swords and those on foot their javelins, and attacked Don Quixote, who waited for them with great calm. No doubt it would have gone badly for him if the galley slaves, seeing their chance to free themselves, hadn't taken it by managing to break the chain on which they were strung. Such was the confusion that the guards, now rushing at the galley slaves who were breaking loose, now attacking Don Quixote who was waiting for them, did nothing of any use at all. Sancho, for his part, gave a helping hand to release Gines de Pasamonte, who was the first to leap forth onto the plain free and unfettered, and who, attacking the prostrate commissary, took from him his sword and the musket. With these, aiming at one and levelling at another, but never actually firing, he drove every one of the guards off the field, for they took to flight — partly to escape Pasamonte's musket, partly to escape the showers of stones the now-released galley slaves were raining down on them. Sancho was greatly grieved at the affair, because he anticipated that those who had fled would report the matter to the Holy Brotherhood, who at the summons of the alarm-bell would at once sally forth in search of the offenders. He said as much to his master and begged him to leave the place at once and go into hiding in the nearby sierra.

"That's all very well," said Don Quixote, "but I know what must be done now." And calling together all the galley slaves, who were now running wild and had stripped the commissary to the skin, he gathered them round him to hear what he had to say, and addressed them as follows: "To be grateful for benefits received is the part of persons of good birth, and one of the sins most offensive to God is ingratitude. I say so because, sirs, you have already seen by manifest proof the benefit you've received from me; in return for which I desire — and it is my good pleasure — that, laden with that chain which I've taken off your necks, you set out at once and proceed to the city of El Toboso, and there present yourselves before the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, and say to her that her knight, he of the Rueful Countenance, sends his compliments. And tell her in full detail all the particulars of this notable adventure, up to the recovery of your longed-for liberty; and this done, you may go wherever you please, and good fortune attend you."

Gines de Pasamonte answered for them all, saying, "What you, sir, our deliverer, demand of us is of all impossibilities the most impossible to comply with, because we can't travel together along the roads, but only singly and separated, each one on his own way, trying to hide ourselves in the bowels of the earth to escape the Holy Brotherhood, which will no doubt come out in search of us. What your worship may do, and quite fairly, is to change this service and tribute owed to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso into a certain quantity of Hail Marys and creeds, which we'll say for your worship's intention, and this is a condition that can be complied with by night as by day, running or resting, in peace or in war. But to imagine that we're now going to return to the flesh-pots of Egypt — I mean, take up our chain and set out for El Toboso — is to imagine that it's now night, when it's not yet ten in the morning; and to ask this of us is like asking pears of the elm tree."

"Then by all that's good," said Don Quixote (now stirred to wrath), "Don son of a bitch, Don Ginesillo de Paropillo, or whatever your name is, you'll have to go yourself alone, with your tail between your legs and the whole chain on your back."

Pasamonte, who was anything but meek (being by this time thoroughly convinced that Don Quixote wasn't quite right in the head, having committed such a folly as to set them free), finding himself abused in this fashion, gave the wink to his companions, and falling back they began to shower stones on Don Quixote at such a rate that he was quite unable to protect himself with his buckler, and poor Rocinante paid no more heed to the spur than if he'd been made of brass. Sancho planted himself behind his ass and with him sheltered from the hailstorm pouring on them both. Don Quixote couldn't shield himself so well; more pebbles than I could count struck him full on the body with such force that they brought him to the ground; and the instant he fell, the student pounced on him, snatched the basin from his head, and with it struck three or four blows on his shoulders and as many more on the ground, knocking it almost to pieces. They then stripped him of a jacket he wore over his armour, and they would have stripped off his stockings if his greaves hadn't prevented them. From Sancho they took his coat, leaving him in his shirt-sleeves; and dividing among themselves the remaining spoils of battle, they went each one his own way, more concerned about keeping clear of the Holy Brotherhood they dreaded than about burdening themselves with the chain, or going to present themselves before the lady Dulcinea del Toboso. The ass and Rocinante, Sancho and Don Quixote, were all that were left on the spot — the ass with drooping head, serious, shaking his ears from time to time as if he thought the storm of stones was not yet over; Rocinante stretched out beside his master, for he too had been brought to the ground by a stone; Sancho stripped and trembling with fear of the Holy Brotherhood; and Don Quixote fuming to find himself so served by the very people for whom he'd done so much.
